COUNTRY LIFE. Not what we would, bat what we must, Make up the sum of living; ' Heaven is both more and less than just I I In taking and in giving. , Swords cleave to hands that sought the plough, I And laurels miss the soldier's brow. par country home! Can I forget The least of thy sweet trifles? Tlte window vines, which claMber yet, Whose blooms the bee still rifles; The roadside blackberries, growing ripe. And in the woods the Indian-pipe? Happy the man who tills the field, Content with rustle labour; Earth does to him her fulness yield, Hap' what may to his neighbour. Well days, sound nights—Oh, can there be A life more rationd and free? Dear country life of child and man! For both the best, the strongest, That with the earliest race began, And has outlived the longest. Their cities perished long ago; Who the first fanners were We know. Perhaps our Babel', too, will fall; If so, no lamentations, For Mother Earth will shelter all. And feed the uuborn nations; Yes, and the swords that menace MOW Will then be beaten by the 'plough. R. Communism paralyses the one and discourages the other by substituting allto-help for eelf-help. Co-operation makes melt-reliant case; communism =bee spools. fed children,"—and then semarks--" To carry cut produitive co-operation, the first and most important ocneideration which every working man ebould take to heart is not to pledge the whole value of his bbour for the means of daily sustenance. Let him once grasp the importance of this, and everything else .will fol- low. If the leaders ef the trades unions would only urge the men to follow this course, they would, indeed, be acting a meal part. Let them exhort their members to band themselves together, and to say, We will no longer pledge the whole of the value which our labour gives to every talustrial enterprise; we will only take part of our wages to money, the rest we will have paid us in shares of the tundertaking en which we are employed.' And from the lay on whicheuch a movement begins to spread throughout the country, material inequality will begin to diminish, and She wealth earners will become the wealth takers, not merely the wealth producers. From that day the working mess will cease to feel that at the end of each successive year he is no better off than he was at the termination of the previous one, ind that his capital,. which is youth, energy, and strength, is constantly diminishing, while he is wasble to replace it by any other equivalent. On the last day of the oid year the rich man may console himself by the thought that though he is a year older he is also more wealthy and powerfaL To the scholar the merry chime of belle which ushers in the new year brings the soothing selketion that he has accumulated a fresh store of learning during the past twelve months. The statesman can think With satisfaction over the measures he has passed which will bring fame to himself and prosperity to his nation for "aerations to come. The only thought, however, which as »our to the working man is that he is a year nearer to- the time when his capital—the capacity to work—will be' exit:tasted. Is it any wonder, then, that a deep feeling of dineontent is to be found throughout the industrial popula- tion? How different it would be if he knew that the past year had added a fresh sum to the capital which would enable him to decrease his manual labour as he advanced in Ifs, and ensure him a comfortable provision for his old age." Justice Scott, who is regarded 29 a competent authority, has written to the Times of India a memoir of General Gordon, from which we extract the Mewing :—The story of General Gordon's career is now UK He is still in the primepf life, and he has already amsemplished enough to make half-a-dozen men famous. It' • le heed to say where the secret lies of his success. He is 4:112212511 of danger, but many other men hold their lives as domply. He despises money, but he is not singular in that Indifference. He is all frankness and sincerity, but these volitire are fortunately not very rare. He has an intense ,blLith, but there are other men who possess an equal trust and belief. Self-reiianee -equal to his own has ensured noose to other leaders. It is, perhaps, the rare combina- tion of all these qualities which go to make him remarkable. 4Wfs men have a kinder heart. His pensioners are many, and are scattered over the world. But with all his kindness he ean be very stern. He has shot evildoers with his own amid, and unflinchingly ordered men to execution by way .otexample. His religion is the most powerful factor in his Actions. Whenever he is in doubt he tune to his Bible. With the English newspapers that Book formed his whole ,Illeary in the Soudan. Bet shrewd common sense is mixed up with his almost mystical religion, and his constant refer- ent* to his Bible, opening the Book at random for guidance is the practical working ef life, has never led him astray. The present writer well remembers the first time he SAW -{beedim. It was in Egypt, at Ramieh, the desert suburb of Alexandria, just at the close of the first chapter of tie Equatorial rule. A slight man, under middle size, of erect military bearing, with a clear-cut face, a small moustache, and penetrating light blue eyes, walked into the room from the back way, apologising in a shy, gentle voice for coming in through the kitchen," be- lessee, you see, I could not find your front door." We sat /bat day for hours, and over endless cigarettes he told me with eloquence how he won over the hostile tribes by justice sad fel: dealing. He paid, he said, for all he took; carried everywhere with him a public petition box, and always read the petitions, helped the weak against the strong, and freed all captives who were being carried away into slavery. He sever went armed, not even when the natives were creeping garangh the long grass, spear in hand, ready to attack when- over there was a chance. Later on he corrected himself *Val the arms, and said, "Yes, I once did sleep with a re- solver by use, but I was sorry afterwards that I did." It was ;seldom he would talk as he did that day. He was generally rather a silent man, low-voiced when he did spealc,l d gentle in all his ways, especially gentle with women and erhOdren. We remember another occasion when, as we sat together, one of the children rushed into the room all tears, became her brother had gone without her. "Never mind, say dear," said Gordon, calling her to him," all will come right. You have your troubles, and I have mine; we must both try to bear them." And he took the child on his knee, and talked to her till she had forgotten her woes. His troubles then were no small ones. His work was all over, and he was leaving Egypt without a word of gratitude from these he had served so well. The Government have even haggled over his arrears of pay. Tan Youiro Coreratavrou.—One of the clTacte!istlos of most young authors, or would-be authors, is their im- great hurry to be accepted, and aidseatilolt grthoeateeh exigenciesur r leasta why their contribu- tion, of the month, should tihtnpbei lbwtcprinted.hhiaei:yethtjaho are ey,a saSTanwhsent i" donh ainnav: etthc nnt the understand e e 2 o l 'hot be in type upon the 27th. I had experienced this feel- ing of impatience myself, and had had cause to regret it. When I was a very tender striping indeed—not more than sixteen or seventeen at most—l had sent an article to the ,Azeople's Journal, and received the joyful tidings of its ac- ceptance. It was the first paper that I had ever had ac- cepted, and I was wild with triumph and delight. Rather gto my annoyance, however, when I purchased the next Satur- day's number, I did not find in it what I looked for. How- ever, I managed to exist for seven days longer without . bursting, bought the succeeding number within the first hour of its appearance, tore it open without waiting for a paper knife—and was disappointed again. Then I wrote to the editor, very calmly and dispassionately, pointing out that there had been a mistake, and begging, in the most courteous manner, that it might not occur again. It did, however, occur again, whereupon I wrote him another letter, not so dispassionate, and in course of post received— most deservedly—my M. declined. With this recollection in my mind, I of coarse felt no surprise at the impatience of contributors. The forms it took were, however, some- times very peculiar. That the subject was as old as the hills did not make the slightest difference. The same anxiety for instant publication was manifested for some essay upon the character of Queen Cleopatra as though it were on a topic of the day; it never seemed to strike these writers that what the world had done without for a thou- sand years or so, it might still do without for another fort- night; they hoped to see their contribution towards the History of the Visigoths "in our next issue," with the word "next" underlined. One gentleman, who had sent us a pressing paper of this kind (I think on the Round Towers of Ireland), was especially unfortunate; he was an Irishman himself, he told us, which however was somewhat super- fluous, for in his precipitancy he had omitted to give his address. A week afterwards he wrote in a great state of ex- citement to know why he had not heard from us, which nothing but the appearance of his Round Towers in print could, in his opinion, excuse; but in this case, too, he gave no clue save the postmark, which was Dublin, to his private address. Then he wrote to say that flesh and blood could Intend such neglect no longer, and that he was coming over to Edinburgh to demand a personal explanation; and still he omitted to say where he wrote from. Eventually he actually arrived, livid and foaming, and on being confronted with his headless correspondence, only burst into a roar of laughter, and observed that it was "mighty queer."—Corn- hill Magazine.

On October 10 the 200th anniversary of the birth (41 Watteau will be celebrated at Valenciennea A drinking fountain in the Place Carpeaux and a statue of Watteau by Carpeaux will commemorate the day. , A NEW KIND OF GUNPOWDER, called brown powder, has been introduced into lirripp's works. It is said to have , been discovered by chance its constituents being the same as those of the ordinary black powder. It only explodes in an air-tight space, and burns without explosion a long time in the open air. It gives greater first velocity to the shot, and can be used with cannon of any calibre. There is less Ismoke attendant on the explosion, and what there is can be more easily expelled. Farther experiments are being made. MOUNTAINEERING.—At the meeting of the Geographical Society in Jane a paper on the ascent of the Himalayas is to be read by Mr. Graham a Scotch gentleman, who is said to have reached a height of 27,000 feet above the level of the sea. There will probably be present at the meeting Emil Boss, the veteran Alpine guide, who accompanied Mr. Graham in his ascent, as he accompanied Mr. Whymper on Cotopaxi and Mr. Green on the Alps of New Zealand. Mr. Graham is understood not to despair of yet reaching the top of Mount Everest, a height of 30,000 feet. A CURIOUS TELEPHONIC EXPERIMENT lately made by M. Hospitaller at the annual meeting of the Paris Physical Society is being much talked about in Paris. Two terminals of a telephone system were placed in the right and left hands respectively (uncovered) of two persons. The two unoccupied hands were then applied, gloved, to the ears of a third person. This gentleman is said to have heard per- fectly under these conditions whatever was spoken through the telephone, though his collaborateurs, who formed part of the circuit, of course heard nothing. This property of the hand to act as a telephone receiver is the more remark. able as the human body has considerable electrical resist- ance.

_ Arte e Storia reports the finding of two candelabra and two basins, buried in the garden of the great Church of Bethlehem. The basins are especially interesting not only for their size (they are 22in. in diameter) but for their shape, which resembles that of ancient Oriental cups, and yet more for the engraving on them, which appears to be the work of a Christian artist between the 11th and 13th centuries. The subject of the engraving is the principal events of the preaching of the Gospel in India and the martyrdom of St. Thomas. Probably the basins came from Edema, to which place, tradition states," the body of St. Thomas was carried. The legend of the acts and martyrdom of the Saint is in rhymed Latin verse. On the candelabra is written, " Maledicatur qai me aufert de loco Sancta Nati- vitates."

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
THE MINORCA.

One of the best breeds for domestic purposes, where the first object is the getting of eggs, is the Minorca, and our ; readers will remember that we have often recommended it. I The more we see of this bird the higher is our opinion of it, as it has all the qualities which go to make up a really me. ful bird, save perhaps one, and that is it does not make one of the beat table fowls. Chickens of this variety are good eating, and grow to a fair size, but we should not recommend them where fowls are lobe much dealt in. They are laying to wls par excellence, and in such places where the first object is to get an abundant supply of large, well- flavoured eggs, then we regard them as the very best breed for the purpose. They are good sized birds, and bear con- finement very well indeed, laying almost as well in confined spaces as when at liberty, so that whilst they will enjoy an extensive run, they can be depended upon, should that not be at hand—a very important consideration—and their black plumage makes them especially suitable for towns or manufacturing districts. They not only bear confinement well, but can be kept successfully on almost any soil, and are very hardy, both as regards the adult fowls and the chickens. They are non-sitters also, and on this account are to be recommended in yards where chicken hatching is not desirable, as there is no temptation to commencechicken rearing. The Minorca is not a large eater, and in places where an extensive run can be given they are found to be capital foragers, so that a flock of them can be kept very cheaply. All these considerations point to it as a most valu- able fowl.

Until a few years ago the Minorca was almost entirely confined to Devon and Cornwall, where it was regarded with very great favour—in fact, being the principal fowl of those counties, as it still is. It is undoubtedly one of the Spanish tribe, and was probably first brought over to the western corner of England direct from the Peninsula, but when or how we are unable to learn. Mr. Tegetmeier mentions that Minorcas were exhibited under the title of " Barbezieux," at the last show in the Bois de Boulogne, at Paris; but we have not come across the fowl in this way. And whether these fowls are still to be met with in Southern Europe has not been stated. Bat it is very probable that they are more like the original Spanish than the birds which we possess, and to which we give that name. Unfortunately Spain is not a favourite resort of tourists, and probably few who have fancy leanings have ever visited that interesting country, so that our information with respect to fowls there is very meagre. They are not bred with any degree et care, and hence the closely defined types of fowls, such as we are accustomed to in this country, are rarely met with. It would be an interesting study to pass in review the various breeds to be found on the Peninsula, with the view of dis- covering whether there are the same varieties as we find here all coming under the designation of Spanish breeds. This, we hope, may be done are long. As already stated Minorca" were up to a few years ago almost entirely confined to the counties of Devon and Corn- wall, but there they were very carefully bred. Reports came now and again of the remarkable exhibitions of these fowls held in that district, and gradually interest was directed towards them; fanciers in other parts of the coun- try began to bay specimens, until now classes are given in all good shows for them, and they are to be seen all over the island. From an exhibition point of view they have been a success, and as the majority of fanciers, whether ex- hibitors or not, like birds that are good layers, they have, as our American friends say, "filled the bill," and hence the reason of their popularity with those who have kept them. And, unless they are spoiled by being bred too fine, or by crossing, this popularity is certain to increase. We shall do all we can to prevent their deteriorating, for it would be a misfortune to allow them to go back in economic quali- ties, as have their brethren the Black Spanish, simply by the exaltation of some point which may add a little to the beauty, but is of no service whatever to the actual value of the breed. It will, however' be necessary that all should carefully watch against any deterioration, and any reduc- tion in the size of body, in the fecundity, or in the hardi- hood of the breed, should at once be attended to in order to prevent such an undesirable result. In-breeding is to be very strongly depreciated, as it does a permanent injury to the fowls by weakening the system. Of the Minorca there are two kinds, the white and the black, bat the former are very rarely seen. They are not unlike White Leghorn' in most respects, the legs, which are white in the Minorca and yellow 111 the Leghorn, being the principal difference. Therefore, in speaking of the Minorca, we are always to be understood as meaning the black variety. The general contour of the Minorca is similar to the Spanish, namely, with a stately upright car- riage, mounted on fine, shapely legs, with the head well drawn back, and surmounted by a large single comb, with long pendant wattles below the beak, and a round, fall, prominent breast. The Minorca is, however, somewhat lower on the leg, and of a stouter, emptier build than the true Spanish. And in the head points the comb is usually very much larger. In fact we regard it as too large, for often in closely kept fowls the head is unable to sustain the large comb, and it topples over on one side. In the hen this is always the case and we prefer to see birds without such huge combs. Breeding could soon reduce this te more reasonable dimensions. But the great difference between the Spanish and the Minorca is in the face. That of the former variety is entirely white, and the object of breeders is to get it as large as possible; but in the latter the face is coral red—hence the name by which it is known in many places, red faced Spanish—with a white ear lobe. The fact that the tendency in fine bred birds is for the white of the ear lobe to spread all over the face, shows to us that at one time the Spanish themselves had red faces, and in the Minorca we always rigidly object to a bird showing white On the face. It would, indeed, be a sorry day for this variety were it to follow in the way of the Spaniels, so far as the face is concerned. And thus we should advise our readers who keep Minorcsa for breeding to put out of the reckoning all such birds as show white on the face. It is not necessary for us here to give any actual results I secured by this valuable breed of fowls, whi,ch we could do I if it were necessary, for they have now established their position. Of course, no one must think that in praising them as we have done we expect they will lay every day, never ail anything, and stand any sort of treatment. They will not do that Bat hens, not individual ones but a num- ber of them, will lay an average of 220 eggs per annum. They are also very hardy, and if fed properly and kept in suitable places are not subject to many diseases, bat they need to be treated in a common sense fashion. With such treatment there can be no question as to their merits, andl we regard them as forming one of the most valuable varie- ties of domestic poultry that we possess. SEASONABLE HINTS.

We are now more than half-way through the month of May, and in all well-managed yards the breeding season will be almost If not entirely over, and when this is so the breed- ing pens should be broken up. It it is intended to breed any chickens for Christmas or the early spring, the pens for that purpose can be made an exception. The old birds should be carefully examined, and those not likely to be wanted as breeders next year had better be sold or fattened off as soon as possible in order to make room for the chickens, which are growing daily in size, strength, and vigour. If there is plenty of room and the hens are laying well, they may all be put in a large house and kept there for a couple of months, but the gentlemen had better be got rid of. Every useless or non-productive bird is a direct loss, and should not be kept where profit is desired, for it takes the profit of one,good bird to pay for each useless one, and means a great waste of force.

DEATH OF AN OFFICER IN EGYPT.—Capt. Humphreys, who on the morning of the 6th inst. was thrown from bis horse and fatally injured, died on Monday night. Owing to the nature of the injuries he sustained, it was found impossible to remove the unfortunate officer from the 'spot where he fell, and he has lain there ever since the acci- dent.

RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon, when there were present: Messrs. Leatherbarrow (in the chair); J. T. Hall, W. Newsome, W. A. Meadows, W. Swi t, J. Leigh, E. Syder, and J Kenwright, and 8. H. Hartley (elerk). RH-APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OF/GLIM—IR accordance with a no ice given at the last meeting Mr. Newsome umved the re-appointment of Dr. Hall as Medical Officer of Health for three years, at en annual salary of £l3O. He remarked that they would all be acquainted with the ability and char- acter of Dr. Hall, and be (Mr. Newsome) had never heard any reports against him. He believed Dr. Hall had per- formed his duties to the satisfaction of the Board.—Mr. Kenwright: It is time we were dropping salaries.—Mr. Hall: The population is increasing and also the wcrk.—Mr. Kenwright asked what work Dr. Hall had to do.—Mr. Hall replied that it was a question of brains.—The motion was then seconded by Mr. Meadows and passed. Tan SANITARY CONDITION or Dmrow Townenns—The Clerk stated on the previous day Mr. Gilbedy and himself inspected Ditton township, to see what should be done to improve the sanitary condition of the township. They found Duke-street in a very bad state, and Pitville-terrace, which had been loudly complained about, required some- thing doing at. They were afraid that if - they went too deeply into the thing it would mean a Very expensive sewerage scheme' and they suggested that the surveyor should take levels of the place, and ascertain where the sewerage would go. It would be a pity if they should spend a lot of money and then found they had not a natural outfit!l for the sewage.—Mr. Meadows moved that Mr. Twist should be instructed to take the necessary levels, and Mr. Newsome seconded the motion, which was adopted. MEDICAL OFFICER'S ttsroter.—The monthly report of the medical officer of health (Dr. Hall) stated that he could again favourably report, no case of an infections nature having been reported since the last meeting. Several cases of water supply were alluded to, after which the report continaedr—The death rate for April is as follows: Bold 00, Cronton 21, Dillon 07, Eccleston 11, Hale 00, Hale- wood 1-5, K owsley 113. Rainhill 11, Spoke 58, Tarbock 11, Whiston 11, Windle no return. INstmeron's Himont —The Nuisance Inspector (Mr. Twist) reported that after examining the cottages near the site of the old mill at Knowsley, which had been referred to at the last meeting, he found there did not appear to be anything exceptional in the locality to cause pollution of the water. The cost of laying 14 inch galvanised wrought iron water pipes, two feet below the surface, from the mains on the hill to a point in Blundell's-lane, near the entrance to Dean's farm, and fixing a cased stand pillar on the site of the old disused well, with drain for waste water, T pipes for private connections, and other necessaries would be about .£l5O. The distance from the mains would be about 780 yards, and the property to be supplied would be Mr. Hat- ton's farm house, Mr. Graham's, and seven cottages. The cottage in School-lane, referred to by the medical officer, obtained their water from wells or neighbouring farms. There was no public supply available, and wells or bore- holes would have to be sunk if a better supply was insisted upon. He had seen and heard from Mr. Swift about the plans of the new asylum, and he promised to bring the matter before the next meeting of the cemmittee.—The re- port was adopted. EMIGRATION OF PAUPER CHILDREN TO CAMADA.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. E. Gibbons and H. Bright and Captain Willis, 30 boys and 20 girls, formerly inmates of the Union Workhottse, signed papers signifying their consent to emigrate to Canada. Mr. B. H. Hartley, clerk to the Board of Guardians, stated that he had to ask their worships to hear the children verbally give their consent to being sent out to Canada. The Local Government Board, he contended, now offered facilities for boards of guardians to send out numbers of children, and last year the Prescot Board of Guardians sent out 30. This year they proposed to send out 50, and the necessary forma had been prepared, it only being necessary for the magi- strates to hear the consent of the children.—The Chairman: What is the limit of the age fixed 7—Mr. Hartley: There ism limit to the age except that the children shall not be over 18 years of age. The Local Government Board had ' issued very stringent, and be (Mr. Hartley) thought proper, 'regulations as to the placing of the children in proper homes on the other side of the water. They required the Guardians to undertake on the part of the children that they had a reasonable hope of places being found for the children. Homes were already awaiting the children, and if they had a larger number of eligible children they could find them suitable places. The Canadians were very anxious to secure the children, and the Canadian Government had entered into an agreement with the English Government to forward an annual report as to the disposal and position of the chil- dren.—The children then came forward and individually stated their willingness to go to Canada, after which the magistrates signed the necessary papers. PRESCOT &nom BOARD.—A monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Clerk's office on Monday evening, when there were present: Messrs. W. Goldsworth, T. P. Hewitt, J. A. Sanders, and IL Cross (clerk). The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed.—The Supervision of the Schools: Mr. Goldsworth, in accordance with notice given at the last meeting, mowed that Mr. Bay- liss be appointed to take charge of, and be responsible for the heating, cleaning, lighting, and due execution of all re- pairs of the schools; and take charge of the premises.—Mr. Hewitt seconded the motion, which was agreed to.— Monthly Return of Attendances 4c.: The monthly return of attendance and fees, showed the following item, in regard to the attendance: Boys' school: Number on books 260, corresponding month last year 233; attendances 8,024, last year 7,284; attendances lost 1,856, last year 1,104, average 218, last year 193 ; and girls' school: Number oa roll 120, last year 121; attendances 3.978, last year 3,471; atten- dances lost 1,022, last year 885; average 99. last year 96. Infants' school: Number on roll 104, corresponding month last veer 85; attendances 3,490, last year 2,568; attendances lost 670, last year 832; average 87, last year 64 —Cows of Children: Mr. Bayliss reported that he had been instructed to prepare a census of the children who had attained the age of five years during last year, and he found the number was 102. He was informed that they would attend schools as follows: Church 32, board 27, neutral 24, private 17, doubt- ful 2.—Tne Chairman remarked that the return would be of considerable advantage to the authorities as showing the number of children wise had attained the school age; and Mr. Hewitt said he' quite concurred with these remarks.— The meeting then Concluded.

Holland and Sir , D. Currie as to the state of affairs in Zululaad, Mr. GLAD- "PIfe said the Government were responsible for the preser- vation of peace and order in the "Reserve," and would fulfil their.._ engagements, but they did not intend to undertake any military interference in the affairs of the remaining portion of Zululand. O'llorres AND TITE SPRAYER —Mr. O'BRIEN made omplaint of tha conduct of the clerks at the table, by ,a,'",ich he had been deprived of the precedence which be had °toed at the ballot for a motion reflecting on the "felonious realms " of certain officials in Ireland aud the attempts of the Executive to screen them. Some expressions which 'riled to imply that the clerks might employ their power 411,. editing the language of motions for the purpose of con- :ring with the Executive to get rid of unpleasant subjects, ought up Mr. GransroNE, who warmly protested agaiust attacks on officials who could not defend themselves—a re.actice which he said had been entirely unknown within kis • Parliamentary experience until the last few years—The SPEAKER explained that the hon. member had lost his pre- cedence because bis motion contained charges which were too vague, and because he had not corrected it until it was too late—Mr. O'BRIEN gave notice that he would make his ' !Mien, attacking certain individuals whom he named, on " vote of credit for the Civil Service Estimates. PENSIONS —Mr. ANDERSON asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether it was true, as stated in the Standard, that he had arranged for the commutation of the Marl- " ugh pension of £4,000 a year into a payment of ,„go '07,000, and of the Penn pension of £4,000 a year into a PaYinent of £67,000; and if so, what was the reason for the Mee of one being 271 years' purchase and the other 161 Y,,ears' purchase.—Mr. COURTNEY (Treasury Secretary). in said the statement quoted was not accurate. The rnts of commutation in both cases were the same, namely, 28/ years' purchase. r_hOLDIERS' WIDOWS.—In reply to Col. Milne Holm and `' ,''rd H. Lennox, Sir A. HATTER said it had been decided that the widows of private soldiers killed in the Soudan or Who died from illness there would receive a pension of 3s a "reek, and is 6d a week for each child of the de- eaced. Similar pensions would be granted to the widows of soldiers in future campaigns.—Mr. Cmariamt-Barisnut- ataE said some provision would be made for the widows Said children of sailors killed in the recent expedition, but was unable to state at present on what scale they would hued. THE MERCHANT SHIPPING BILL. CusarnicatalN, in moving the second reading of the Merchant Shipping Bill, expressed his regret that he had • tot been able to call the attention of the House to the sub- le_et at an earlier period. The great obstacle to a satisfac- `"Y settlement had been the irritation which prevailed r ' eg all classes of shipowners founded on an impression at a general and undeserved imputation had been cast ;Ton their character as honourable men. In that, however, neY were under an entire misapprehension, and if any word ;1 his had produced such an impression he trusted that no ....acting arising from it would be allowed to prejudice a good "11511„. • He had made two distinct allegations—first that 'wire were black sheep in shipowning as in other trades, and reondly, that any law whicb enabled a man to make a pro- at out of the loss of his ship and its Crew was contrary to lannd policy. Other trades had been interfered with by the Le- gislature for the protection of the persons employed in them, !Ild in the case of the shipping trade the necessity for inter- Terence was even greater. Since this Bill was introduced there had been held a great meeting of delegates of the shipping trade in the Cannon-street Hotel, London. Of the IS delegates present at it, 47 were shipowners in their own Ilan"' Having looked into the matter, he found that in the Est five years those 47 shipowners had lost 65 ships and 367 lives, and that nine of the 47 had lost 35 ships and 177 lives. ne was not going to found any accusation against those centlemen. Perhaps every one of those casualities was from causes beyond human skill and human foresight. But the trade of which such a statement could be made, and in which the lose of life was so terrible, could not come for- Yard and assert its independence of criticism. At a meet- lag of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce, a captain had dernounced the bill and said it ought to be kicked out of the House or Lords, and taking a copy of it from his pocket, he ;few it on the floor and stamped on it. Be found that since 1;77, that was in seven years, Captain Hatfield had owned hips and had lost eleven. (Sensation.) Adding together tb °° Periods for which each vessel had been owned, be found that this gentleman had lost actually one in three of the .a. ine he owned, and this was the gentleman who went to the meeting of the Liverpool Chamber of Commerce and said Mr. Chamberlain was hampering a great industry. Mr. Maclean: I rise to order. I wish to know whether the right hon. gentleman is in order in making a libellous attack upon ai gentleman without giving him previous Potice.—The &MAIER, without noticing the interruption, *died npbn Mr. CRAMZERLAIN, who said he took these figures from Public documents, so that there could not be the slightest doubt about their accuracy. (Hear, hear.) Ile proposed to Igloto first that the loss of life at sea was excessive, and was rather increasing than diminishing; secondly, that it was due to causes which were more or less preveutible in their' Ilharacter ; thirdly, that all impartial authorities agreed that an increase of care and precaution would diminish these losses; and, lastly. that the state of the law and the Practice of the trade undoubtedly tended to relax the "dinary motives of care and afforded a temptation to negli- gence. In 1862 the steam tonnage of this country was 637,000, in 1872 it was 1,537,000, and in 1882 it had risen • 3,835.000. At the same periods the sailing tonnage had 'leen 4,335,000, 4,155,000, and 3,586,000 respectively, Bo that there bad been a total increase from 4,872,000 tens in 1▪ 862 to 6,921,000 in 1882. From a return giving the total toes'of life in connection with British merchant ships re- gistered in the United Kingdom, without reference to pas- sengers, it would be found that, dividing twelve years into .three periods, the figures were—for the first three years, 0,314 ; for the second, 9,181 ; for the third, 7,612; and for the last three years, 9,553. The decrease in the third period folMwed immediately on the Plimsoll agitation. In twelve "cm 36,000 eeamen had suffered a violent death. On the question of Midermanning he found that in 1871 the ton- Lag, wits 5,573,000, and in 1882 6,679,000, an increase of culler cent ; but in the same period the number of men rPloyeel had fallen from 218.000 to 211,000, a decrease of Per cent.' If men sent their ships to sea deliberately in !der to get, the insurance, banging would be too good for 15111. It should be made impossible for any man to make Profit out of his loss. It was a scandalous law that allowed E Profit to be made out of over-insurance. The right hon. gentleman meat proceeded to explain the main principles the bill and the amendments that had been agreed upon te the conference he bad had with shipowners. The main Principle of the bill was that a policy of insurance should be a policy of indemnity, and that an insurer should not gain bY the loss of the thing insured. (Hear, hear.) The bill Proposed to extend to ships provisions similar to those of the Employers' Liability Act, which gave compensation fcir all damage or injury or loss of life arising out of the negli- gence of the employer or defect in the equipment of his works or in the condition of his machinery, and prevented the employer from pleading the doctrine of common em- ployment. Finally, Mr. Chamberlain concluded a speech of more than three hours and a half in length by defending his proposals against the charge made against them that they would drive the shipping trade to foreign-countries, and appealing to all sections to support a bill which em- bodied not all he desired to do, but all that he found possible. (Cheers.) , Mr. MACIvEn opposed the bill, which, he maintained, was introduced under false pretences, and Mr. C. PALMER, Who also opposed the bill, urged that the subject, and especially the charges against the shipowners, should be inquired into by a Select Committee or Royal Commission. Mr. E. STANHOPE, speaking for the late Government, said they would abide by all the declarations they had made on the subject. , Canvassing the provisions of the bill, he doubted the expediency of extending the Employers' Lia- bility Act to the Mercantile Marine, and strongly opposed the proposal to open 'valued policies. But of the other Proposals for preventing over-insurance he generally ap- Proved. He thought the bill quite unsuited for a Standing Committee., Mr. WirtiEwsow approved of the bill, and believed it would be acceptable to the country. Mr. GonST could quite understand that there were certain Persons who were anxious to tint this into a personal quer- ' rel,with the President of the Board of Trade, but no one who heard the speech of the right hon. gentleman could say that it contained "monstrous and fantastical" charges against the shipowners. He complained that the bill bad Leen watered down to please the shipowners, and appealed to the President of the Board of Trade even now to pluck up Cour- -441,3 altd,eubmit the bill to the House in the more generous form in Which it was introduced. He cordially tupported the second rending. . Mr:E.iSmorts also supported the second reading, in order that the kill might be referred to a Select Committee, where the controversy started by the President of the Board of Trade Might be fully investigated. On the motion of Mr. E. Cramer, the debate was ad-, burned. MrecumaNmons.—On the motion' of Mr. HOBE= the Summary Jurisdiction (Repeal, dic.) Bill Was referred to a ,„Select° Committee.—On the motion of Mr. BURT, the Canal • eats Act (1177) Amendment Bill was read a third time, and referred to a Select Committee. div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDA.V. TO Lord. Chancellor took his seat at 4-0. milkoLLANaorrs.—Viscount Hampden, the late Speaker of the amp, of Commons, took the oath and his seat —Lord 1/automat; ,armed the second reading of the Secretary for Scotland Bill, ,:vhich, after some conversation, was agre*d to.—Oa the mak.: of the LORD CHANCELLOR, a bill for the abolition of the office of Lord Privy Seal was read a second time.—Lord SvHays•Dlo:( and CAMPBELL had placed on the paper a motion declaring tit was not desirable to move the Wellington statue from LOMon until the public had an: g opportunity of seeing the moninnen by which it was to be replaced. Lord Gl:azimut, on the ,'ound that a similar proposal had already been decided npOtt .by the House, moved that this resolution be not put. On divieon the Motion was negatived by 78 votes against A 2. Lord STB.ATHRDIIN then moved his resolution, and after some Conversation it was withdrawn in favour of one nractic.Ally to the same effect moved by Lord Da Roe. On a division this last was carried by 66 votes against 44. The Duke of RUTLAND asked what the Government were going to do. Lord GRANVILLE smilingly remarked that he "was not at liberty to say."—Their Lordships adjourned at half-past Seven. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIESDAI. TRH CREW OF THN NISERO —Mr. GLADSTONE, answer- ing a question about the crew of the Nisero, said there was reason to fear that if any steps were taken in a summary manner against the Rijah, whose prisoners they were, be would put the men to death. The Government fully recog- nised it to be their duty to take whatever steps they could to release the men. IRELAND AND THE FRANCHISE BILL.—The House re- sumed committee on the Franchise Bill, taking up the dis- cussion of Lord Claud Elamilton's amendment (moved by Mr. Brodrick) excluding Ireland from the benefits of the RANnow CHURCHILL said the measure was a trumpery little affair,ln no way worthy the designation of • great reform bill. He thought it might be allowed to go up to the I ords, where, no doubt, it would be received with the consideration to which it was entitled. On the particular point before the House he differed from tome of his friends, and would be obliged to vote against the amendment. He thought the position the Government had taken upon this question was on the whole wise and statemanlike. The noble lord, after a passing sneer at "the ingenuous and fertile mind "of Mr. W. H. Smith. commented upon the absence of Sir Stafford Northcote. Lord Claud Hamilton said the thought that had passed through his mind whilst he listened to Lord Ran- dolph's speech was, "what is the noble lord driving at ? " If this was to be a specimen of the Democratic Toryism of the future he for one respectfully declined to follow any such doctrine or any such leadership. The Liberal party, the noble lord said in a lofty passage, were content to follow the infatuated man who led the country into disgrace abro td and into anarchy at home, Before five years were over they would bitterly repent the course they had adopted when they supported him in bis work of completing the disruption of the Union. Lord Edward Cavendish said there was in this speech much of the old tone of "ascend- ancy" which would do nothing to reconcile the bitter differ- ences that had so long existed in Ireland.—Colonel Torrust- HAK denounced the speech of Lord Randolph Churchill.— After some words from Mr. Dickson Mr. CHAPLAIN attacked Lord Randolph for his speech, and quoted an address de- livered by him in the recess, in which he solemnly warned the country against the unification of the Irish franchise with the English.—Mr. STATELEY HILL opposed the amend- ment, asking the House to "be just and fear not."—Mr Ewart and Mr. Macartnev, the latter "speaking as one of the loyal North of Ireland men," supported the amendment.— Mr. LAsoccirsun suggested that the Liberals should meet the conspiracy of loquacity on the other side by a confederacy of silence. Lord George Hamilton, whose prolonged remarks were interrupted by cries f ir the division, supported the amendment. Sir Patrick O'Brien delivered ale animated speech, understood to be in favour of the bill. His observation that there were in the House some persons who called themselves Irish members, whereas his impres- sion was that they were American members, led to some in- terruption, to which Sir Patrick responded with alacrity. " Order ! order!" was cried. "Sir," Sir Patrick in lignantly retorted, "I am not in order," subsequently explaining that he meant he was. Mr. Kenny distinguishing himself by ironical cheering, Sir Patrick turned upon him and an- nounced that he had his eye on the young sea serpent of County Clare. The Chairman interposing, said the bon. member was not in order in using language of that kind. "Then," said Sir Patrick, "I withdraw the young sea ser- pent." Once more he was turned aside from the flow of hi argument by laughter on the other side. "I hear a twinkle," he observed. The continuance of the remark woe drowned in shouts of laughter, and as Sir Patrick did not return to this branch of the subject the House was left in doubt as to the precise meaning of the reference. At twenty minutes to six the House divided, when the numbers were For the amendment 137. Against „ 332.

div.head: Majority for Government 195.
div.p: Majority for Government 195.

Sir S. Northcote absented himself both from the debate and the division, many Conservatives following his exam- ple. Sir R. Cross, Mr. Gibson, Mr. W. H. Smith, Mr. Plan- ket, and Mr. Cavendish Bentinck were the only members of .the front bench who supported the amendment. Lord R. Churchill and Mr. Gorst voted with the Government. At seven o'clock the sitting was suspeeded. 1 On resuming at nine o'clock the House was immediately counted out. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WRDNEMAY. The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes past twelve o'clock. RAILWA:f RAMS.— Mr. B. SANcELsow moved 11l new standing order, the object of which was to allow a Chamber of Commerce or Agriculture to appear before a committee on bills dealieg with railway rates affecting their district. He spoke of the desirability of putting a check, in the public interest, on the arbitrary action of railway companies as shown before the committee on Railway Bates—Mr. GREGORY seconded the motion. He said the subject was one of the most important to the agricultural interest, and as the railway companies had a monopoly facilities should be given for an equitable adjustment of rates.—Mr. Lama, in the absence of Sir Joseph Pease, moved, as an amend- ment, that where an application is made by a railway undertaking fir parliamentary powers attention should be lirected by the Board of Trade to the proposal, and in the case of an existing company to the existing rates or fares with a view to their consideration by the committee, and that persons affected by such rates and fares shall have a loess staltdi before such committee.—Mr. BoLpow seconded the amendment—Mr. CHEMBERLEIN said, as to the amend- ment, that he objected to the functions of the Board of Trade being increased. As to the motion he admitted that a revision of railway rates was necessary, bat he objected to it being done by a perpetually changing tribunal. The revision, too, ought to be made in favour of as well as against the railway companies. He intended to proceed with the Government Bill for carrying out the re- commendation of the Committee on railway rates, and, that being so he hoped the motion would not be pressed. Ile I proposed to throw upon the railway companies the onus of " bringing forward in a bill a new classification of maximum rates, and a bill of that kind might be referred to a strong hybrid Committee, with power to take evidence. He moved the adjournment of the debate.—After some remarks from ,Bir R. Cross, the debate was adiourned. - ABOSNEION D,.—Mr. DODSON moved that next day bil- ling AllEelliiOn Day, Committees should not sit until two o'clock, and should have leave to it till six o'clock.—Mr. ,ARNOLE opposed the motion —The House divided, when there v,oted for the motion 93, against 37. littert L&ROIIRERS.—Mr. MOLLOY moved the second read- ing of the Labourers (Ireland) Act 1883 Amendment Bill.— Other members having spoken, Mr. TREYELYAN stated that under the Act considerably ever a quarter of a million would be borrowed IT Irish unions from the Treasury. He 'thought it impossible. therefore, to say that the Act had conferred no benefit on Ireland. Dealing pest with the provisions of the bill, which he regretted had not been laid before the House at an earlier period, he urged against abolishing the Confirma- „tory Act of Parliament, which was only needed in opposed 'ages. As to clause four, dealing with the repair of cot- tages, it would be a dangerous precedent to apply the Arti- ians' Dwellings Act to labourers' houses in Ireland. It was a power too great to give till a vigorous and searching in- quiry was made, and such an inquiry would be made under the Royal Commission on the Dwellings of the poor.—Mr. 'PARNELL said this was the third Bill of this session which was supported by Irish" members and opposed by the Go- vernment, and,H Mr. Trevelyan had chosen to turn himself 1 into a deliberate obstructor of Irish measures, be could not complain if the Government met with a little retalia- tion.—ln answer to Mr. Molloy, Mr. TRWIELYEN stated that he would consent to refer the subject of the housing of the poor in Ireland to a Select Committee. The House divided, when there voted for the second reading, 75; against, 138; ;majority against, 63. , MB PROPOSED CONFERENCIL—Baron DR WORMS gave notice that on going into Committee of Supply he would move—‘ That, having regard to the Conference on the 'affairs of Egypt, this House is of opinion that any arrange- ment giving to Continental rowers any right of control ' over the administration of Egypt will be detrimental to the Interests of England and India, and render nugatory the Sacrifices made by this country for the tranquility and good I ;he government Hone so adjourned dEjourngYpte.; at six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THIIIISDAV. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. WEST LAnCaiRIBB RANamt.—The West Lancashire ' Railway (Extension) Bill (New Title) was read a third tlintl•l Quaranows.—Mr. J. I. CROSS informed Mr. Stagg that 1 F the sanction of the Secretary of State for India had been given to the construction of the Quetta Railway, and that the work would be executed with due despatch. The CHAN- i CIILLOR of the ExCaNucER was asked if he would consent to the appointment of a Select Committee to inquire into the whole question of the tobacco duties, and the right hon.l gentleman replied that, considering the magnitude of the duties, he was not prepared to consent to the appointment of such a committee. Mr. BRAW-LRFEYRB stated that be was unable to carry out the recent resolution of the House of Lords with reference to the removal of the cotton' statue of the late Duke of Wellington from Hyde Park to Aldershot. MonnoINTS ON Tim MLLE.—The Pause MnrisTEß, in reply to a question, stated that Lord John Hay was making arrangements for patrolling by steamboats a certain portion of the Nile. The steamers would be from the Khedive, and there would be a small company of British sailors on board; but the question was one purely regarding the ad- ministration of tits interior of Egypt. Iwere using every effort to communicate with General Gor- don. In reference to the movements of Admiral Hewett, it was stated by Lord E. Feraseattmcz that the Admiral reached Adowa on the 6th of May, and Was awaiting the arrival of the King of Abyssinia, who was expected on the 12th of May. bir W. Hewett had, reported that he was being treated hospitably. CIVIL Seamen EsvuukrEs.—The House went into Com- mittee on the Ciml Service e climates, and en a vote on account being moved Baron II DE WORKS moved its reduc- tion for the purpose of asking that the Government, before they were engaged round the Conference table on the Egyp- tian question. shoule. give some explanation as to their pro- jects.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in the course of his reply, stated that, according to the view of the Government, there was not the slightest apprehension that the interests of England would be prejudiced in the Conference. The object of the Conference WAS to consult the interests of England and the interests of all the Powers, and should the conclusions arrived at touch money matters they could not be given effect to without the consent of the House. lie could only repeat that the Government adhered to the basis of the Conference as it was originally stated. As to the reconstitution of a dual control, there was very little reason to apprehend that the Government would propose the re- newal of an arrangement which, although it did good at the time, had been productive of disaster to the country.—Mr. J. LOWTHER Wished to know whether in the event of any attempt being made to enlarge the scope of the Conference beyond the pare and simple qttestion'of finance, the British representatives would be instructed to withdraw.—The PRIME Mneurrat answered that the Government could' not attempt to extract from the Powers an assurance that they did not intend to enlarge the scope of the Con- ference without conveying an imputation upon the other Powers and being guilty of a want of courtesy towards them.—A discussion followed on the policy of the Post-office towards the Telephone Companies. The subject was introduced by Mr. GRAY, who complained that the Post-office Department had made a monopoly of the telephonic business.—Mr. SLAG° remarked that his con- stituents felt a very special and deep grievance. In the great commercial centres as soon as capitalists came forward and established a telephone exchange the Post-office authorities came down upon them and charged 50 per cent. on their gross receipts. He could not conceal from himself the conviction that it was the intention of the Department gradually to obtain possession of the telephone system.— Mr. FAWCETT stated that he hoped soon to make changes which would be satisfactory. THE CREW or THE Ningo.—Mr. STOREY said he wished to call attention to a matter that seemed to him to be more important than the problematical advance of Russia to India. , The hon. member went on to narrate the story of the cap- tivity of the crew of the Nisero at the hands of a rajah in Sumatra.. These poor men had now been in captivity seven months, and practically nothing had been done to secure their release. He would press upon the noble lord the Under Secretary for Foreign AffairS that some active measures should be taken in this case. Lord E. Fri-Minima said papers would be laid on the table , • to-morrow containing the correspondence between Her Majesty's Government and the Dutch Government and the • Rajah, and when the House saw those papers they would see how completely unjustifiable were the remarks of the • hon. member for Sutherlands that the Foreign Office had done nothing.—After a few words front Mr. Ashmead-Bert- I lett, amid cries of "Divide," the subject dropped. • Mr. PARNELL having drawn attention to the retention of extra police in the city of Cork, was informed by Mr. Tux- ! VELYAN that the extra police could not be removed at • present. t The House continued sitting till a late hour. e

to an intrigue of the Greek and French Commis, who have left Massowan in order to be present at the n'tgoefations at Makaki. It,wae the same Greek who thwaned General Gordon's mission. Two British officers were insolted in the market-place by soldiers of the Governor. The people were rude and offensive. The admiral stopped leave to enter the tows. Allula returned with letters from the King to the Admiral, saying:—" I send you Has to assist in counsel and in getting provisions. As your Excellency has come to make friendship between the two kingdoms you must be in no hurry to return. lam coming soon." There is no re- ference to the treaty, the terms of which are :—Firetly, Massowah to be a free port; secondly, the country of Bozo ' Senheit to belong to Ethiopia; thirdly, the ruler of Egypt to give facility in the appointment of an Abuna ; fourthly, King John to give every assistance to the garrisons of Kalabat, Kasala, and Aroadib, allowing them to withdraw through his country with safety; lastly, the difficulties arising with Egypt to be settled by the arbitration of England. A mission from the Beni Amer Arabs praying for protection against the Mandi has been favourably re- ceived by the King. Commander Rolfe has arrived.—Darly News. TdE PRINCE OF WALES AND THE FENIANS. PARIS, SATURDAY —The Prince of Wales remains at the Bristol Hotel. Two more persons, alleged to be Fenians, are stated to have called at the Hotel Vendome, and in- quired whether any communication existed between that building and the Bristol Hotel, both being in the same block. The two hotels are watched by detectives.
FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR. TouLox, SATIJRDAY.—The man-of-war Le Scorff is pre- paring to leave for Madagascar, with 115 men and 302 troops.

THE KRASZEWSKI TRIAL. BERLIN, MONDAY.—Te-day the Supreme Court of the Empire at Leipsic passed sentence on the Polish poet and novelist, Kraszewski, and on his accomplice, Capt. lientsch, late captain in a Prussian regiment of infantry, who for the last week have been on their trial for treason, in that, to the great damage and detriment of the German Army and Em- pire, they furnished and offered to furnish secret military information of various kinds to several foreign Govern- ments, especially to that of France. Captain lientsch was found guilty on the main counts of the indictment against him, and sentenced to penal servitude for nine years, with deprivation of civil rights for the same period ; while on Herr von Kraszewski was passed the milder, but yet, for his age and position' terribly severe judgment of 3it years' im- prisonment in a fortress. MAJORITY OF THE CZ AREWITCH. ST. PETERSBURGII, SUNDAY. The Czarewitch to-day attained his sixteenth birthday, and ay Russian law his majority. The event has been signalised here by various Court and State ceremonies, and by a popular fete on the Field of Mars.

TURKEY. FATAL FIRE IN TURKEY —1,600 BUILDINGS DESTROYED. CoarxrArnmeLn, MONDLY.—A. great fire occurred on the 17th inst. at Bet Bazaar, in the province of Angora. Owing to the strong wind prevailing at the time it was impossible to stay the progress of the conflagration, which destroyed 950 houses, 544 warehouses and shops, 11 mosques, 15 schools, nine khans, nod 146 other buildings. Eleven per- sons perished in the flames. The cause of the catastrophe is net yet known. An inquiry is being held by the authorities. CossvarrtwortE, TIIESDAY.—The verbal note from Lord Dufferin and M. de Nelidoff requesting the Porte to give instructions to the Ottoman delegates for the delimitation of the new Turco-Persian frontier, rendered necessary by the cession of Khotour district to Persia, is couched in friendly terms. The Ottoman Government maintains that the British and Russian Commissioners in fixing the frontier line were guided by a Russian Map, which the Porte declares to be incorrect. The Porte demands that the question should be settled at Constantinople, while Lord Dufferin and M. de Nelidoff contend that the Commissioners should proceed on the spot. WEDNESDAY.-- A telegram received at Constanti- nople from Eklimiaeitn, dated 17th inst., states that Arme- nian delegates for Russia, Turkey, Persia, and India have met for the election of the future Catholicos. The Rus- sian representative declared that Russia would leave the delegates full liberty of action. The names of the two can- dates receiving the greatest number of votes will be 'sub- mitted to the Czar's choice. CONSTANTINOPLE, TRUESDAY.—The Porte has issued a circular dated the 20th inst. to the foreign Embassies mad Legations, calling attention to the manner in which several Consulates abuse the diplomatic privileges of exemption from Customs duties.

FORI 14.'GN NEWS. EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. • THE PROJ ECTED EXPEDITION. Canto, SATIIRDAY.-11 is generally understood here that the successful sorties of General Gordon reported by the refugees who recently arrived at Assouan, and mentioned by Lord Granville in the House of Lords, are simply those re- ported by General Gordon himself in his published des- patches. CAIRO, MONDAY.—Mr. Clifford Lloyd will not leave till next week. Confirmatory news has been received to- day of the treasonable tendencies of the Governor of Don- gola. His garrison is under command of a Turkish officer not much more to be relied upon than be is himself. No- thing, therefore, now really stands between the insurrection and Wadi Haifa. The Commissariat here has received orders to prepare for an English expedition. One of the first necessities on which they will be engaged will be the pur- chase of 12,000 camels, and for which saddles will have to be manufactured.—Standard. CAIRO, MONDLY.—The news of the capture of M. Cozzi while escaping from Berber by hostile Arabs, near Abu 'lamed, appears to be confirmed, although the British dip- lomatic agency has received no information on the subject. Two companies of Egyptian troops have left Assouan for Korosko and Wadi Haifa. A torce of artillery will leave on Thursday for Assouan. CAIRO. MONDAY.--M. CUZZI was not British agent at Ber- ber. He was simply employed by Genera,' Gordon to trans- mit messages. Several refugees have been captured, so it is probable that he is one. Telegrams continue to be received regarding the serious state of the country around Dongola and Abu flamed. The Mandi's emissaries continue to ad- vance, and are received with open arms by all the villages and their sheikhs. It is doubtful whether the Governor of Dongola can be arrested.—Dailv News. Assomax, MONDAY.—Tne Arabs have captured the Go- vernment magazine at Abu Hamad. Alarming rumours have reached us from Korosko. The Arabs are reported to be advancing. One company of Egyptian infantry, under Captain Eager, is going up in the morning. Arzir Moham- med Ebdullas is considered the most formidable military sheikh connected with the Mandi's movement. His presence near Berber proves that the Kordofan forces have reached the valley of the Nile. Colonel Duncan, commanding at Assonan, has sent to their homes 1,890 Khartoum and I Berber refugees. The Egyptian troops here are in aR excel- lent state of discipline, armed with Martini rifles, and appear reliable.—Daily News. The Pall Mall Gazette asserted on Wednesday night that the Cabinet had "practically determined" to send a relief expedition to Khartoum early in the autumn. The relief force, which is to consist of "at least" 10,000 men of all arms, will be under the command of Lord Wolseley, and will land at Suakim and march on Berber. The construc- tion of a military railway between Suakim and Berber is " indispensible," and will be at once taken in hand. The Pall Hall Gazette says that these assertions will be speedily verified by events. The troopship Humber and the hired transport Dunlnce, just returned to Woolwich from Egypt, are ordered to be re- tained for another voyage to Alexandria. It is understood that special freight lists are to be prepared for them, with a view to the requirements of an expedition to Khartoum about two months hence. Mach activity is said to prevail in the War Department in inquiring into the strength and condition of regim-nts standing high on the roster for foreign service. The Admiralty have invited tenders for I engines to be used in small boats; thirty in all will be re- quired. Each boat will be fitted to contain with ease thirty men, and will be constructed of the same pattern, but of less draught than those used by her Majesty's transport ships, for embarking and disembarking. The boats, the materials for which are now ready in the Government Docayards, could be fitted out and put on board the transport ship with- in two months if necessary. If any of the tenders for engines are accepted, orders will immediately be given for the con- struction of the boats to be commenced. The Daily News is in a position to state "with autho- rity" that no decision in regard to action in the Soudan, going beyond the declaration made by Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues in the Cabinet in the debate on the Vote of Censure, has been taken. Inquiries, of course, have been I 'set on foot, and preparations for eventual contingencies have been made, but no determination has been arrived at either formally or in substance. ' ATTEMPTS TO COMMUNICATE WITH GENERAL GORDON. The Daily Telegraph correspondent at Cairo telegraphs the following items of news under Tuesday's date :—Every effort is being made here to communicate with General Gor- don. Messengers conveying despatches leave almost daily. They are paid beforehand. with a promise of liberal reward if they bring back General Gordon's answer. The despatches confided to them are otten hidden in quills, and tle messen- gers take every possible precaution to prevent the discovery Icf these receptac.es upon their bodies if searched. Colonel Kitchener telegraphs favourably from Assouan respecting the Abadeh tribes. He says that 1,000 Abadeh warriors have appeared on the frontier, and will very shortly be in position ort the line between Korosko and Shilibat, a Red Sea port between Berenici and Elba, thus protecting the Egyptian frontier. Three hundred Fagarrah left Assouan for Korotato yesterday. CAIRO, Wunstsion.—Telegraphic communication is now restored as far as,De ,beh. The_ Governor of Dongola has been peremptoHly ordered to witbdraw at an early date with the garrison. He is, however, beyond the reach of the tele- graph, having proceeded to Meraweh. ATTACK ON SUAKIM.• sokunt, WRDNDSDAY.—Yesterday, Captain Brewster and his twenty police being absent at the opening of salt mines at Rowyeh, a party of rebels stole a thousand sheep close to the forts: and the news arriving too late, the cavalry pur- suit proved a failure.—Times. Busxna, MONDAY.—Daring last night a party of about two hundred rebels fired upon the town for more than an hour, but took to flight directly the British landed. Two of the townsmen were slightly wounded. All is now quiet. Colonel Charmside telegraphs from Suakim that the Egyptian soldiers behaved well during yesterday's fire, and took up their posts without noise. He found everything in excellent order. One native was wounded. The rebels never approached nearer than from 200 to 300. yards outside Suakim. When the British landed everything was finished. MADRID, SONDAY.—The Saragossa newspaper states that. the coart-rnartial held on the fourteen officers and men *ho deserted from Santa Coloma at the end of last month has sentenced one of the prisoners, a major, to penal servitude for life, a lieutenant to twenty years' imprisonment, and the remaining officers to twelve years, The private soldiers were acqaitted. The Government are about to send reinforce- ments, consisting of two battalions of Marines, tcf the Philip- pine Islands. OPENING OF THE SPANISH CORTES. MADRID, TUESDAY.—The fourth Cortes of the Restora- tion was opened to-day by the King with the usual cere- mony. The Royal speech which is a document of great length. commences by an allusion to the recent attempts at disturbance of the peace, and establishes a connection be- tween the Spanish Anarchists and those of other countries. Nevertheless the Government, having confidence in the nation and itself, does not intend to modify in a restricting sense the existing laws. The speech adds :—" With the greatest pleasure I inform you that the relations between Spain and the Holy See never were so cordial as at the pre- sent time. I have great satisfaction in stating that the re- lations with all foreign Powers are friendly, without any question whatever marring the existing harmony." THE CAPE.—ANGRA PEQUENA. CAPETOWN, MONDAY.—In to-day's sitting of the House of Assembly, Mr. Upington, the Premier, in reply to a ques- tion, said that the Colonial Government were strongly opposed to the establishment of a Foreign Power at Angra Pequena, and especially to the creation of a penal settle- ment•—lntelligence received here from Stellaland states that the British flag has been hoisted at Vrijbarg with the consent of the Volkersad, amid public rejoicings. BitaLlN, THITIODAY.—At a general meeting of the Ger- man Colonial Association, a resolution was adopted for transmission to Prince Bismarck exprelsing gratitude and satisfaction at the Chancellor's decision to protect the economic interests of Germany in the Congo territory, and recording the firm confidence of the meeting that he will succeed in frustrating any steps hostile to German interests that might be contemplated by other States.

DISASTROUS FIRE NEAR WARRINGTON.

A disastrous do occurred at Sankey Bridges, near WAN rington, on Wediaseday afternoon, at the chentical works belonging to Messrs. William Longsbaw and Sone. As moat as the outbreak was wherved information was despatched to the Warriogton Fire Brigade Station, in Heath-side, and the alarm bell was immeilitely rung. It being then shortly after two o'clock in the afternoon, and the mirket being crowded, a large number of people quickly assembled near the Brigade Station to watch the prepara:ions made for de- spatching assistance to the scene of the fire. The reel and hose were at once got out, and several members of the brigade proceeded to Sankey Bridges, reaching the chemisel works in less than half an hour after the alarm had been given. On arriving there the hose was got into working order without delay, a plentiful supply of water being oh- ta toed Mfrom the canal which passes through Sankey Bridges, in the immediate vicinity of essrs. Longshaw's works. Is addition to the hose from Warrington, an engine was lent by Mr. Ridgway, who has a manufactory in the neighbourhood. but owing to the inflam- mable nature of the building and stock the efforts of the firemen, seconded by a number of willing volunteers, were of little avail, the portion of the works in which the fire occurred being completely gutted in a Yew! short ?pace of time. They were, however, successful in preventing the flames spreading to other buildings. In all there were four or five hoses playing upon the fare, but the engine of Mr. Ridgway, being soinewhat out of repair, was not of any very appreciable service, water having to be brought to it in buckets from a brook near by. The works are divided into two parts. One part coneists principally of brick, and is devoted to the manufacture of catholic acid. The other part was constructed chiefly of timber, and in it was carried on the manufacture of nitric acid and nitric lead. It was in the middle of this latter portion of the works that the outbreak occurred, and as a good south-west breeze was blowing at the time, the conflagration rapidly spread, gam- ing a complete hold of this portion of the building, which was entirely gutted in less than half an hour aft.tr the arrival of the hoie and engine. The material being of an entirely inflammable nature, burnt freely, and the ref ters i fell in quick succession. The part of the works n lhich the fire recurred was completely destroyed, as was also the material in the process' of mannfueture. A large number of spectators were attracted to the spot, and watched the progress of the fire. Water was poured on to the smouldering debris until evening, and t'.C. Philips re- mained on the spot until all was considered safe. Unfor- tunately, the building is not insured. The amount of dam- age is not yet definitely stated, but persons competent to judge say chit it cannot be less than £2,000. How the fire originated is a mystery, but it is reported that Mr. Long- sbaw himself has expressed the opinion that it was caused by smoking amongst the men. During the progress of the fire one of the firemen, named Smith, accidentally placed his leg in some chemical preparation, and sustained injuries which, it is hoped, will not prove serious. Re was taken home in a cab.

EDGE GREEN PRIMITIVE ME rISODIST CREEL.—The Edge Green Primitive Methodists celebrated their Sunday School anniversary on Sunday last. In the morning aa address to teachers, parents, and friends was delivered by Mr. J. Buckley, of Leigh. Sermons were preached alternoos and evening by the Rev. J. Slater, of Liverpool. All the services were well attended. A number of anthems, ac., were rendered by the choir, and the collections realised the sum of £22

LIBERAL. MEETING. On Monday evenieg, a well attended meeting of Liberal' was held in the Golborne Congregational Schoolroom, nudes the auspices of the Gelborne and District Liberal Associa- tion, when an address was given by Mr. W. R. Kennedy, el Liverpool. Mr. W. Mitchell occupied the chair, and was supported by Colonel McCorquodale, and Mr. C. Pewen (Liberal agent for South-West Lancashire).—The Chairman said that the object of the meeting was to support the Government both in its home and foreign policy, and to give an expression of the opinion of the meeting on the ex- tension of the franchise to the counties—a question than which he thought there could be no better, as it meant he widening of the basis of representation for the people. (Ap- plause.) He was old enough to remember the passing of the 1832 Reform Bill, and had a vivid recollection of the state of the times then, which he proceeded to contrast with the benefits enjoyed by the working population at the pre- sent day. He felt satisfied that the great improvement that had taken place had been mainly brought about by the 'superior class of men who were put into the House of Com- mons in consequence of a larger basis of representation. (Hear, hear.) It was easy to say that at that time there was a representation of the people, but it Was one in name and not in reality. They might draw their conclusions from the fact that at the time he referred to the adjoining town- ship of Newton sent two members to Parliament, and the now important city of Manchester had then no represents- tion at all. It Was some time before the effects of the change wrought by ths passing of the 1832 Reform Bill began to be felt. Then with the superior class of men returned to Parliament came the repeal of the corn laws and the advancement of the free trade question. The more extended basis of representation that Doe Government wag endeavouring to pass would extend the franchise to the agricultural classes, who would return men to the Howse of Commons who would pass such measures as would make the land as free to buy and sell as any other article in the market. (Applause.)—Mr. W. Jackson then proposed "That this meeting of the Golborne and District Liberal Association expresses its sincere thanks to the Government for its determination to press forward the County Franchise Bill, and its confidence in the policy of the Government at home and abroad."—Mr. Yates seconded.—Mr. Kennedy, in speaking to the resolution, said that the present was a time when everyone who cared for the cause of t.lberelism should be prompt in coming forward in support of the present administration. The cause required and deserved on the part of those who called themselves Liberals that constancy and steadfastness that would enable them to repel the attack of the enemy and win victory. There had been an attack in the attempted vote of censure that was recently moved by Sir Michael Hicks-Beach that was something like the attack and temporary success of the Arabs when they attempted to get into the British square at Tamanieb. But he thought that the result had in both cases been the same, and that no amount of alarmist prophecies would prevent them showing at meetings like that that they had theeame confidence in Um Government that they had when they placed them in power four years ago. (Applause.) The question of the extension ef the franchise was, he said, one of the most important that the country had had to consider for many years, and he believed it to be a measure—as they would all believe it to be—not only of justice but of expediency also. (Applause.) Of justice because, as many of them knew, they would in that very county of Lancashire, under the present state of things, have men on one side of a street haring votes and men on the other side, equally qualified by property, net having votes. Tnat was a glaring injustice. The proposed measure in that county alone would add something like ; 70,000 votes to the register. It seemed to him to be mon- strous that that measure was required to give votes in that icounty to 70,000 men, who were at least as well qualified as the bulk of those who had votes already. It did not breams the dwellers in or near towns to forget that, white it was a matter of justice to redress the inequality that at present kept the suburban dwellers without votes, it was even more a necessary act of justice to give a voice to the great agri- cultural population of the country. The artisan classes in the great cities had votes, but there were large traces of the country, where men, perhaps not learned, but wise felt the want of maoy things, had at present no means of approaching through the constitution of the country that great assembly which could decide whether those things ,• should be given them or not. He confessed that looking at ,Ithat phase of the question alone ,it was enough to make him an ardent partisan of the measure which the Government r WAS now about to introduce. (applause.) But it was not merely the remedying of an injustice or the giving of votes to the agricultural population that was to be considered.' Surely the indirect benefit that would follow from the , sure being carried was a weighty matter, and one open , which they could not expect any Tory to agree. One thing that had often struck him Was the absence of any means at ! I present existing for the education of the county member. - There had been a vast difference for the past twenty years in the positions occupied by the member for the borough' . and the county. The member for the borough had to know and did know his constituente.—knew the class with whom he had to deal, and by whom be had been elected. In most oases the county member represented a large area the electors of which were never, or scarcely ever, collected together te discuss his actions or advise him upon the futare,aud be was too often the nominee of one or two great families, ec their nominees, with the passive assent of those who depen- ded upon those families for their subsistence. It seemed to him that members could have comparatively little weight in the administration of a Liberal Government, or of te. country, who went year by year to Parliament without hue, ing had their education at the bands of their conetituests. They wanted reform in local Government and taxation—% subject which lay very near to the root of all projects in the agricultural districts. He advocated one council for oue county, do that they would have the best men of all ranks and classes taking a share in the administration, which would be the means of checking One of the greatest and most important expenses in the country, contending that with separate bodies they could get no coherent account of how cost was incurred, and that they could not get the best men to represent them. The thorough reform of the land system, he said, was also urgently needed. The present lend system was a relic of past times which must be pc rid of. Mr. Kennedy proceeded to speak at length on the land question and Ireland, and again referred to the Fran- chise, concleding by urging the Liberals to remain united and work for the cause.—A vets of thanks to the chairman, proposed by Col. McCorquodale and seconded by Mr. Powell brought the meeting to a close.
