div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 24, 184.

SIR GILBERT GB EENALL tells us he is "an - odd old fellow," and as to this at any rate there is no denying that he is right; he is so odd and so old that his friends might with advan- tage look after him a little more than they seem to do. He has a way of his own—in some things; he does not for instance devote much time to advocating the Three R's; he cleaves rather to the Three F's—Flood, Fishing, and . ii Flogging, for at the Conservative Ward : Meeting on Monday night he devoted himself entirely to these extraordinary topics. Taking them in order, we are led to infer from a perusal of the speech that " Flood " has reference to a working-man of that name, who has rendered himself obnoxious to the Conservatives by daring to have an opinion , cf his own on matters political. We gather, too, that he is in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, as to . which Sir GILBERT is careful to tell us that he does not believe they have one better cus- tomer than himself; and then he adds—" Let • the London and North-Western Directors, if they have the courage, say that their ridicu- lous ' Flood ' shall no longer trouble me." Now, what does this mean? If we do not , wholly misunderstand Sir GILBERT, and if we are wrong we shall be glad to be set right, it conveys a threat, it involves a species of in- timidation, which is as humiliating to a great Railway Company as it is discreditable to a great brewer. It is putting on "the screw," ' as it seems to us, and in a bold bad fashion. And yet in the same breath he says he is "in favour of the interests of the working-man." Was there ever such a contrast between pro- fession and practice! If the working_men of ' Warrington will tamely tolerate such an in- dignity, all we can say is that they deserve to be the slaves of such masters as Sir GIL- BERT GREENALL. Oh, but he is going to let them fish in the Reservoir—if somebody sends him " some small fry." and—another "if "—if the fish increase He has some- how discovered that working-men want fish and have votes, and, as he wants votes and has fish, he evidently thinks that an exchange can be agreeably effected. It is true he would give the matter an air of philanthropY by providing that the payment for fishing shall go to the Infirmary. But it won't do; not to put too fine a point on it, the transac- tion is altogether too "fishy." The whale ef public favour is not now to be caught by Sir Gilbert's sprats; he offers them too late in the day, and under circumstances which may lead ultimately to a trial before one of her Majesty's Judges. at which something may be said about bribery and corrupt prac- tices. Ito whether he had, as stated by us a fortnight !go, at any time voted for the retention of ' 'flogging in the army. There could be no', mistake about the question and there can be , none as to the answer. Sir GILBERT in re- Vying said: My dear fellow. I would not' flog, whatever they say. Flogging! I never voted for flogging • I never will vote for flog- ing." How gushingly kind he is! It must have been shocking to his nerves, with his tender rerard for the working-man, to have h suggested that he could possibly think of Itch a thing. Well, he either has, or he has not voted in favour of flo3-ging in the 41r147; and if he hasn't we will humbly con- fess our sins and apologise to Sir GILBERT 'GREE/rALL for having made a statement 'Which he evidently regards as derogatory to _;his character. It is a matter fortunately Which is capable of proof—one way or the 'Other; and, notwithstanding that the benevo lent baronet ought to know what he has done 'in the past for the working-man much better than anyone else we venture to re-affirm our statement. "Facts," Burns says, "are chiels Ithat winna ding, and downa be disputed," and 'here are the facts. On the 2.6 th of March, 1878, when Lord eeaconsfield was in power, and Sir GILBERT was a mer'nber of the House "Commons, Mr. O'CONNOR POWER moved to reduce the number of lashes that might be inflicted under the Mutiny Act from 50 to io. On that occasion Sir GILBERT GREENALL voted for the retention of the 50 lashes; the soldier—the working man of the army—thus ROI the full bem-fit of his vote, and of the ,l,ash. Ten stripes Bah, give him fifty! On , the same day Mr. O'Coxigoit POwER moved that the punishment of flogging should not be inflicted twice in the same year, and when it was put to the vote Sir GILBERT GRF,ENALL voted against the motion—that is to say, he Voted not only in favour of flogging in the army, but for the " cat " being administered twice, if it was thought fit, in the same-year. And why not'? Does he not tell us that he ,has been "a pretty consistent fellow " all his ,• life? Next year (July 17th, 1870 Lord HAR- , lINGTON raised the whole question of cor- Poral punishment on the consideration of the Artily Discipline and Regulation Bill, and he nioved an amendment to the effect that " No , - bill for the Discipline and Regulation of the Ttny will be satisfactory which provides for the permanent retention of corporal punish- 1 utent for military offences." The question 'Was put, after considerable discussion in winch Lord HARTINGTON was strongly sup- Ported by other members of (he Liberal party, and Sir GILBERT GREENALL voted against the motion. To put it plainly, he said by his vote that the " permanent " retention of flog- ging in the Army was a 'satisfactory" thing. L'ir GILBERT says as to those who question "is votes that they should "state the time, and place, and circumstance." This is exactly what we have done, and we trust he will Profit by reflec ing on this choice bit of , biography; meantime commending to his notice Hotspur's advice to Gendower —" Tell truth, and shame the devil"

MR. CHAMBERLAIN has added to his repu- tation by the, manner in which he introduced the Merchant Shipping Bill, the second read- ing of which he moved on Monday night. e had before given ample evidence of 'lleiditv in statement and power in argument, I,3iit on Monday night he displayed a compre- hensive grasp of a great subject, and a mas- , terY of the most complicated details which, I,aken together, reveal the highest capacity or statesmanship. So many reckless and tt„rlfoUnded charges have been ,flung at him Inat, with the material before him, it would have been -ea.y to punish his opponents by ,eXPosure .of their calumnies; but he felt that he had a higher duty to discharge, and directed :himself therefore to so laying the measure before Parliament as to avoid that irritation and opposition which would endanger its passing. He studiously avoided exaggeration and sensational statements, but, aS he himself pertinently remarked there was nothing in the statements so sensational as !he facts. It may well be ,asked how it °aPpens that within a few years of the pass- mg of a bill to protect the live 3 of our sea- ken it has become necessary to begin the tllsk again. It seems only the other day that Mr. PLussorl. stood on the floor of the House of Commons, and created an extraor- dinary scene by his excited denunciation of t,he BEACONSFII,LIY Government for proposing tO throw the Shipping Bill overboard—the result being that, under pressure of public °Pinion, the Government were compelled to Proceed with the measure. The bill 'passed, "nd was for a time beneficial in its operations; °lit selfishness and greed have been too many for it, and a change in the law is again obso- lutelely necessary. It.is pretty as a figure of sPeech to think of The sweet little cherub that site up aloft To keep wretch for the life of poor Sick;

_ . tut as a matter of fact poor Jack's life is nenl.g. sacrificed year by year•hy sending him , " rallt 'at rotten, overloaded hulks that go to the .°ttorn under the stress of the first storm that -weaps over them. It is appalling to reflect that,over 3 000 lives are lost yeally—many of tAllernirom ctuses that are clearly preventible. . ‘l•3 the law stands, shipowners are too often Permitted to have a greater interest in their 1 . .--I.liPs sinking than they have in their return- , Ing safely to ha,bour. This notorious evil is i ; the outcome pure and simple of over-insur- ance; it is monstrous that it should be so, but there is no denying the fact. When the news came the other day ,of the loss of the Plorida, there was not a fall as might natu- rally be vtpect, dof the shares of the line ; 'I)n• the contrary, they suddenly advanced .'.Plenty-five net cent., the instant conviction haing that the Company wmild gain rather than lose by the loss of the ship. Andif this ' 4tan, be the case with a well-managed line, needs DO ghost come (torn the grave to telhus that there are shippers,olthebaser sort 110 habitually -take advantage of the present 'efective state of the law as to over-insurance In order to prcfit,by the worst of calamities at B.ea• We have altered the law as to the Insurance of children and adults on land so 18 to;check gambling in human life; but ltt.°ln the facts laid ,bare by the President of "e 13oard of Trade, there is ten-fold more .„ 'end ofzimilar protection for the men "that rdown,to the sea in ships, that do business great waters." Now that the nation has ttlin set its hand to the task, there should be itn holding back on account of the protests of 1 'c'se who are interested in maintaining the Itltsent discreditable and disastrous state of flilBs. What are we to think, for instance, n the dramatic action of Captain Hatfield, t:10 threw the bill upon the floor of the • I„,,4'erneol Chamber of Commerce, when we `l.,Tn that "since 1877—less than seven years i Captain HATFIELD has awned as ships, and :II the course of that time has lost eleven of aser° 1 ' Is he to be taken as an authority 11.t0 what is best to be' done? IThe usual penalty of ss. and costs was imposed.—Thomas I Flood, 12 years of age, stepson of John Keating, was com- mitted to St. George's Industrial School, Liverpool, until he has attained the age of 16. On Sunday special services were held, and on Monday evening, what , was termed a . banquet "was given. A whole sheep, two !rounds of English beef, with ham, was provided, and a con- siderable number of people assembled to partake of this , substantial fare. Subsequently an entertainment was , given under the presidency of Mr. R. Peacock, and there was a good attendance. 1 RUNCORN Scnocm BOARD AT Worix.—At the -Runcorn 1 Petty Sessions on Monday, the following persons were each tined 51 including costs, for negleeting to send their children ' regularly to school :—John McDonnell, King-street; John i Antrobus, Wilson's-row ; John Henry Molyntaux, York- street; Alice Shaw, Cavendish-street ; William Price, Stone- : street ; William Clatten, Cinal-street ; Peter Johnson, Stone- ' croft ; Joseph Dutton, Zion-place; James Canliffe, Bridge- water-street: Mary Kennedy, Parr's-square : litnnah Torn- -1 kinson, Duke-street. ' 1 DRSTRUCTION UV 'PROPERTY IN WIDNES —Complaints ' have frequently been made of the wanton destruction of I • cottage and other property in Widnes by gangs of unprin- cipled Alien and women and mischievous youths. The Ipolice, inspired by the Local 'Board, are going to make a determined attempt to put a stop to the depredations, and a Icase was brought before the magistrates on Monday. Brid- get Maly:lion was charged with having on Saturday after- noon been drunk and wilfully damaged a house in Wilson- street belonging to Mr. J. Midwood. P.C. Evans proved 1 the charge of drunkenness, and Mrs. Harrison, living in i Nelson-street, stated that she was 'looking through her win- , dow on Saturday afternoon, ‘• ben the prisoner c‘me up in a i boisterous manner and smashed several panes of glass with t a stone. The prisoner ,violewly ordered her (prisoner's) ; husband out, al leging.that she was harbouring him.—For titsing drunk and disorderly the prisoner was fined liffs and 'costa, and for the other offence 5s and costs and the damage. 1, In default of payment, she went to gaol for a month. OAILAND-STREET V7ESLEYAN GOSPEL TEMPERANCE ' MISSION, WIDNER.—A. .service of song entitled . John Tregenoweth,hiemark," was given in 0 tkland-street school- roam, on Monday evening, in connection with this mission. There was a good audience. Mr. Clark, of the Hollies, Dillon, presided, and in a short speech expressed the plea- sure it afforded him to be present that evening. - He was glad.,to do his beat for the cause they had so much at heart. It WAG absurd for people to think they could not live with- out intoxicating drink, lie stood before them not as a pledged teetotaller nor a " blue ribboner," brat nevertheless a etanach teetotaller, and he should be glad to see large numbers signing the pledge and dunning the " bit of blue." The musical service was rendered Zn an excellent m inner by a choir composed of members of the mission. Mr. John Harper cenducted, and presided at the harmonium. Mr. T. S. Swale Was the reader. On the motion of Mr. Henry Rickard. seconded by Mr. Frederick Harper, votes'of thanks were accorded the chairman and reader'. A collection was made in aid of the funds of the mission. had lost annually one in three of the ships he 'owned ;" and he may well observe that such a trade is best describe& in sailor parlance, as "selling ships to the underwriters." What, again, can be more suggestive than the fol- lowing statement:—" In r 869 Mr. GRAY, the Assistant Marine Secretary to the Board of Trade, made a Teport upon the loss of life in the North Sea. He pointed out that there vrire 220 Swedish steamers uninsured, and tint of these only three were lost in so years. There were zi b English steamers engaged in the same trade, and of these 17 were lost. That is to say, that .the lost ships have been nearly six times as great with the insured." , There is no gainsaying this and other evidence which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN so copiously fur- nishes, and we are driven, however reluctantly, to the conclusion that a considerable number of our British sailors perish at sea year by year because certain callous and cowardly landsmen are enabled to profit by the circum- stances of their death. We do not say that they send out "floating coffins " fioping that they will go to the bottom ; but we do say that they are careless of human life, and that they are play- ing a ghastly game when they allow a vessel to goto sea knowing that they will gain rather than lose by sailors and ships never being heard of more. The principle of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S bill, as he himself states it, is "that it is a wrong, an inexpedient, and an immoral thing that a man should be able to make a profit out of the loss of his ship and the lives he has in his charge;" and it seems to us there should be no difficulty in making this, as he seeks to do, the basis of a reform in shipping law. But the bill goes beyond this ; subject to certain regukitions arising out of the necessity of distinguishing between responsibility attaching to the owner of a ship at sea, and a proprietor of works on land, the bill proposes to give sailors the benefit of the Employers' Liability Act. In this way if it can be proved that there has been negli- gence in sending a ship out in an unsea- worthy condition, and the ship sh3uld after- wards be wrecked, the families of the sailors who are drowned will have a claim for com- pensation. Thus, if a shipowner under the bill is madeto realise that any policy he mayobtain will be void, in-so-far as it is in cxcess of the value of his ship, and that he may also be liable to pay hundreds, perhaps thousands of pounds in the way of compensation, it is rea- sonable to infer that, in his own interest, he will take care of his ships and take care of his men. This is exactly what is wanted, and the nation ,should be contented with nothing loss. A rich and highly organised class interest may make great stir in the way of opposition. but that opposition will meet with the contempt it merits when it is found, to be fos-ered by shipowners who have fre- quently been found t'ouilty of the practice of over-insurance. We are ready to acknow- ledge In song and story the industry, endur- ance, and fidelity of our brave seamen; they are not a class of men to thrust their troubles before the world, but none the less are they deserving of sympathy and right treatment, and the least that we can do is to protect them in their dangerous calling from. the thoughtlessness cupidity, and culpable neg- ligence of some of those who send them to sea

The staring is nearly .£8 per 100 bales, or on the whole cergo nearly f. 200 HALTON PARISH CHURCH SCHOOLS.—Tne Rev. The collections amounted to near'', £l6. Tits CURIOUS ROBBEStY FROM A WIDNES PUBIAC•HOUSE. --At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Sir. John Davies,tbe landlord of the Queen's Head Inn, Lugedale, applied to the magistrates that the I9s 6d which his wife I.ad given,to the. prisoner John Mooney as change, should be returned. It will be remembered that the prisoner was fined £3 and costs for the robbery.— rbe Bench informed the applicant that they hail no power to make such an order as the money had gone into the county treasurer's lands; and the Clerk ad- vised him to be more careful in the feture when giving change, and to apply to the man who had taken the 19s 6d to return the money. TllB CORNERMEN NUISANCE IN WlDNES.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington atid Sir. Ileffirook Gaskell. jun., Patrick aloylen, John Devitt, Jobe NIcG rail, and Je,emiale Buckley wee charged with obstructing the footpath.—P C. Snowden stated that on Friday t tee 9th inst. he was on duty in Ann- ' street in company with P.C. Fryer, when he site the defen- dants standing on the footpath from a quarter past six to a quarter to seven. During that time several people had to leave the footpath. Tee defendants had been warned several times, but they had igoored the warnings. There were great complaints m ide in the neighbourhood of this practice.— Superintendent Berker said Movlen hid been 18 times before the court, Devitt 16, Metirail five, and Buckley one. The defendants were loafers about street corners and there was no getting them off the footpath.—Buckley was fined 2e 61 costs and the rest each 5s and, costs, or. in default, seven days' imprisonment. ROBBERY FROM A WIDNEs LODGING-HOUSE —At Widnes Police Court on atondey, before Messrs. G. Pilkington and H. Gaskell, jun., James McKinley, a labourer, and William Ashton, a joiner, were charged with steeling a shirt, value 3s, the property of William Jones, a lodging-house keeper, Lugsdele-road. On the 16th inst the prisoners were lodging in the prosecutor's house, and Ashton obtained some pota- toes from the landlord on "trust," as he was hard up During the afternoon the prisoners left, Ashton guine through the back yard where the shirt was haegine, and McKinley through the front door. In a short time the shirt was missed, and Ashton returned to the house with some money, and offered to pay for what he had had. He was given into the ensue'', of P.C. Davie, and on Saturdey evening McKinley was apprehended by P.C. Collier. He was then wearing the stolen shirt, and resignedly said he should have to suffer for it—The prisoners were each sen- tenced to 14 days' hard labour. DISAPPEARANCS OF A CHESHIRE BANK MSNAGER.—Mr.• Walker, chairman of the Cheshire Backing Company, has issued a circular to the shareholders. He states that in reference to the proposed am dgemation and formation or the Cheshire and Lancashire Banking Company the regis- tration bad been eff .cted, and the resolutions for adoption were ready to be passed within fourteen days, when upon the very lan day "extraneous difficulties arose which proved to be insurmountable' and the proposed amalgamation fell through." The Chairman of the Company then proceeds to show what these difficulties were. The situation, he saye, was aggravated by the disappearance of the generd manager, Mr. Crabb, who left his post on the 2nd of April, and has not since been seen. An investigation of the books has shown a considerable unantherised overdraft of his private account, in addition to his having fraudulently discounted worthless accommodation bills. The bank 111 stated to be in a position of entire solvency, but as a matter of prudence the directors have decided to make a call of £1 10s per share. . THE ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY: DONATION FROM THE Qtnater.—A meeting of the Exectaive of the Loctl Committee of the Royal Agricultural Society was held on Saturday at Preston, the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw) pre- siding. After some routine business had been transacted, the question of the form of prizes to be offered at the forth- coming show to be held at Preston, was discussed, and eventually a sub-committee was appointed to consider the matter and report their recommendations. An intimation hal been received from the Cnancellor of the Duchy to the effect that her Majesty has been graciously.pleased out of the Duchy revenues to give a donation of £lOO to the local fund.—At a meeting of the leadieg agriculturists of Nor- folk, held at the Agricultural Hall, Norwich, on Saturday, a letter was received from Mr. Jenkins, secretary of the Royal Agricultural Society, announcing that the society's show would be held in the eastern counties in 1886. The Prince of Wales has intimated his willingness to become president of the society in that year if the show were held at Norwich. It was determined to call a public meeting to take steps to secure that object. The Prince of Wales will not attend the Shrewsbury show. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINSr A FARNWORTH GROCER —M Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Charles Taylor was summoned for having in his possession a pair of unjust scales.—Superintendent Barker said the defendant was a provision dealer at Farnworth. He visited his shop on the 19th May and, examined the counter scales. He found they were three drachlts against the purchaser, and subeequently discovered a piece of lead placed upon the iron under the plate upon which the provisions were placed to be weighed. After he had removed the lead the scales were perfectly cor- rect, and would turn with a small piece of paper. The lead had evidently been placed there for profit. He inquired of the shop boy who had placed the lead there, and he replied that he had by the orders of his mistress.—Mr. Ming on : What eort of a business is it?--Mr. Barker said the defend- ant did a large business. He kept a butcher's shop and a gro6rs's shop, and was one of the chief tradesmen in Fern- worth. These scales were in the grocer's shop. On the 24th January last year defendant was fined 40s and co ts fer having lightweights, and on several previous occasions he had been fined for breaches of the Measures Act and of the Bread Act —The defendant, who was represented by his manager, was fined £3 and costs 12s. The PRESTON BANK FRAUDS: ARESST OF TULLY.—The Preston Guardian of Wednesday says :—" A special tele- gram, which we received list evening from ?(w York, an- nounces the arrest of Mr. 'Gerald Thomas Tully, who was up to the 23rd of October last the mile-manager of the Preston Banking Company, Limited, and whose disappearance on that date, after perpetrating a number of serious frauds and forgeries, caused much commotion in this town and district. Mr. Councillor Joseph Toulmin, m 1.?.. of this town, left Preston two months ago on a visit to relatives in the United States. Having completed his tour he retuned to New York prior to embarking to-day in one of the Cunard steamets for England. He telegraphs to us last night that as he was walking along Broadway yesterday he perceived a gentleman who clesely resembled Mr. Tully. Having satis- fied himself beyond doubt as to his identity, he promptly called the assistance of the police, and had -Mr. Tully arrested. Mr. 'Fully was taken before a magistrate, and sufficient evidence was given by Mr. Toulmin to warrant the detention of the prisoner. In accordance with the request conttined in the telegram, we communicated with the chairman of the Bank Directors, Mr. Whitehead, J.P., and a meeting of the Board was immediately summoned. There the fact of the arrest was announced, and it was 'resolved to put the law in force with the object of bringing the prisener up for trial in this town."—Mr. Teulmin, it may be added, is a member of the firm of Livesey and Tout- min, Preston. A LIVILY WOMAN AT Dipron.—At Widnes 'Police Court, on Wednesday, Mary Flannery, a married woman, living at Ditton, was summoned for treateniog to assault, beet, and ill-treat Squire Heys, a blacksmith, of the same place.—Mr. Knowles defended, and pleaded not guilty.— The complainant said on Thursday morning, the 15th May, he went into Peter Ireland's house to do some work. Mrs Flannery followed him, and "called him for all the dirty, drunken, lazy scrawls" sbe could put her tongue to, and threatened ‘;'" what she would do for him." When she had done talking, he said "You are quite right, Mary, jowl your head agtinst the wall." "What," she asked; and here- plied " Bay and straw." In answer to another excited query, he said "sude," whereupon she threw the hatchet produced at him and then a whetstone, subsequently run- !ling at him with a saw. She said she knew he was under a bond, and she would make him break it before he left the cotrage.—Crose-e'xamine'd by Mr. Knowles : Witness denied that he ever said that Mrs. Ftannerv'e bead was addled, or that she ware fele heir.—Jes. Taylor and Richard Harri- son corroborated.—Mr. Knowles Informed the Beech that Mrs Flannery grime time ago bad a serious attack of typhus fever, aid it had had :an effect upon her constitution. She was a very excitible woman, and some of the people in D.tton, among whom was the complainant, took a pride in ageravating her in every manner possible to commit some offence.—Mrs. Flannery was called, and denied that she ever used threats to Heys, and said she threw the hatchet and weetstone not at him bet at the floor. —She was bound over te keep the neaCe fer one mouth, herself in £lO and one surety of £5---A ellen:ens against Mrs Ann Heys, the wife of the complainant in the last cise, for using de- famatory language to Mrs Flannery was then beard.— Several witneeses raving been examined, the defendant was bound over in .rwrilar earetice to Mrs. Flannery.

A lam BICYCLN Rinz.—Mr. J. IL Adams, accompanied by Mr. Torn Moore (" Bicycling News"), Started from Land's' Eud last Saturday morning for the purpose of riding to John I o'Gtoata, the nethermost point of Scotland, in the shortest possible time. Adams' full diatatice for the first day was 1234 miles—a grand ride. Leaving Exeter last Sunday morning, for tbe second day, at the early hour of 6-20, Mr. Attains rode wits Collampton, Taunton, and Bridgewater to Bristol, where at the Royal Talbot, Mr. Moore was met at 3-45. After dinner both rode on to Gloucester, 35 miles, shirting at 5 pm, finishing at 8-30 p.m. Third day: Adams left Gleucester at 6-20 again, and made the best ef his way through Tewkesbury and Worcester to Shrewsbury. Here, after stopping for dinner, a start was again effected, and Whitchuich reached at seven p.m. Here Mr. Moore again turned up. and both rode on ts Tarporley, making the day's ride 112 miles. 'RUNCORN AND THE SI/IE CANAL.—The most intense sat- isfaction is expressed ae: the fact that the Manchester ship Canal Bill has passed the committee stage of the House of Lords, most people concluding that there will now be no diffieulty in it.,passing the House of Lords and the House of Commons. The intelligence was first made known in the town ay a telegram received by Mr. Charles Timmis, about three o'clock; and shortly afterward, tradesmen were to be seen in groups discussing the news. There is not the slightest doubt that if the works are commenced trade in Runcornswill receive a great impetus. The entrance to the canal is to be made a short distance above Ve Old Quay, and it is estima el that upwards of a million pounds will be spent here on docks alone, while there will also be the cut- ting of the canal ant the estuary works. Toe general re- joicing at the event was fitly emphasized by the firing of canons at various works in the 'own. In Widnes, as in Run- corn, the observation upon every persons lips was—" The Bhip Canal Bill's passed," and the news was banded with hearty satisfaction although the effect of the undertaking will not have the the SAM influence upon Widnes as upon Runcorn.

DEATH OF 1. MINISTER FORMERLY OF Rttelconee. The Rev. A. Howson, Congregetional minister, whom 1 death occurred at Keswick, yesterday w ek, will be re- membered by those whose memories carry them back cver a period of nearly twenty years. The rev. gentleman when ifaihe prime of his life, was appointed to the pastor- ate of Bethesda Congregational Chapel, and gave, more than ten years at the beet part of his men- hood in promoting the spiritual welfare of the two towns of Runcorn and Widnee. Ile was associa- ted with the church of the former place during some bf the more, eventful periods ,of its his. tory. Mainly through his exertions a branch of the Independent Church was established in Widnes as early as 1888, but Mr. Howson had left the district before his labours were consummated by the erection of a handsome and substantial chapel there. It was during the •period of his pastorate that the present schools connected with Bethesda Chapel were erected at a cost of £5OO. Later, the organ was built at a cost of £4OO, while the chapel WAS renovated to great advantage and at considerable cost. In all of these undertakings the deceased gentleman took a prominent part, and his posi- r lion gave him the opportunity of subscribing munificently ' towards their accomplishment. He was further placed in the happy position of seeing the whole of the chapel and school property relieved of all difficulties in the shape of trust debts, an achieve.nent which his efforts largely helped to bring: about. The deceased gentleman was of a genial disposition but unobstrusive, and bad a large circle of admiring friends in Runcorn and ‘Vidnes. He was uncle to the Rev. Dr. Hannay, secretary to the Congrega- tional Union of England and Wales, and came to Run- corn from West flertlepool, having previously laboured at Heslingden. While at Runcorn the health of Mr. Howson completely broke down, and he WAS advised to retire from the active work of the. ministry and .travel for some time. Mr. Howson took the advice of his friends, relinquished his connection with Runcorn about 1887, and after 12 months' travel on the Continent was restored to a better state of health. Being a. Keswick the pastorate of the church in that town was offered and accepted, which Mr. liowsm held up to the time of his death. The deceased gentleman was in his 71st year. MUTH OF tsCPRRINTENDENT WILLILMSON, OF 110:1- CORN —lt is with great regret that we caronicle the death of Mr. Sarricel Williamson, superintendent of the Runcorn division of Cheshire Cmaty Police, which took placs at half-past eleven on Thursday morning. For a period of three months Mr. Williamson bad suffered from a complica- tion of disorders, the principal disease being bronchitis, and he had received every aid that medical skill could suggest at the hand of Dr. MacDougall. On Saturday evening the candition of the deceased was regarded as so critical that Dr. Glynn, of Liverpool, WAS celled in, but that physician held out slight hopes of recovery, and on Tuesday era. Wit- liainson's tile was despaired of. Mr. Williamson joined the Cheshire Constabulery on the 15th March, 1859, and as a cmstable was stationed at Crewe for several years. The intelligence and sagacity that he broUght to bear in die- charging his duties was such that in 1371 he was promoted to the rank of detective-inspector at Chester witheut filling the intermediate grade of sergeant. On leaving Crewe the deceased gentleman was presented with a valuable gold watch and al bert guard, the inscription upon which is as follows : —" Preseuted to Detective-Inspector Williamson by Mr. Hill, auctioneer, and 300 friends, for energetic services ren- dered to the tows of CrOwe. April, 1873." In his capacity as detective, Mr. Wffliernsoe won a high reputation as a sagacious and able officer. He was en.aged in entny im- portant mysterious criminal cases, and He displayed a re- markable arritude for collecting evidence and solving criminal problems of a most intricate description. His ser- vices in connecion with the murder of P.C. Green at S and- Web, and of Mr. James Beech, of Bechton, will be remem- bered; while in an intricate case of manslaughter at North- wicb, some years arm, be WAS warmly commended for the Part he played in bringing the culprit to just,ce. In 1878, Mr. Williamson was made superintendent at Runcorn, and at this town, as in other parts of the county, the courtesy and kindness that he displayed in the perfortntence of his onerous and responsible duties won hitn the esteem of all classes, while through his ability and tact be enjoyed the confidence and respect of the magistrates. The deceased, who bad only strained his 48th year, leaves a widow and two sons to mourn his loss. We understand the funeral will take place on Monday. During the deceased gentle- man's illness, Inspector Hollingworth has acted as superin- tendent, and will do so until a successor is appointed.

THE DEFAULTING WIGAN ACCOUNTANT. John Yates Mawson, formerly of Runcorn, accountant and sharebroker, King•street, Wigan, who absconded about two months ago, arrived in Wigan in custody early OR Wednesday morning, and was .brought before the magis- trates at the ordinary sitting of the court. Rawson, when he ab.,conded, was a member of the Wigan Town Council the secretary of the Wigan Provident Permanent Building Society, and the secret try of the Wigan Trainways Corn- pany. After his departure the books of these two concerns were examined, and serious defalcations discovered, the total cl.tici<ncy in the C 1.5 t) of the buildin,r society being put down by the professional auditor at £7,800 'Dune warrants were issued for his apprehension, and subarquently he was traced to San Sebastian. M. de Brunet, the British vice-consul there, communicated with Mr. Webb, the ebief constable of Wigan, and eventutlly the authorities at SAn Sebastian, acting MI the petition of the British Charge d'Affaires in Nl4drid, caused Mawson ta be apprehended. Information of this fact was sent to Mr. Webb, whereupin the Wigan Watch Committee instructed him to fetch 'slew. son from Spain. Owing to the delay in getting the neces• sery ptp.-rs from the Foreign Office and the Spanish authori ies, Mawson was locked up over three weeks at [San Sebastian. . . _

The first chug° against Mawson was that of the• Lanc- ashire and Cheshire Miners' Permanent Relief !ociety, that he, being entrusted as agent with certain moneys belonging to the Right lion. the Earl of Derby and others as trus‘ees of the society, with directions in writing how to apply the same, did, as each agent, in violation of good faith and con- trary to the terms of the said directions, unlawfully c invert the sum of £l3B 183 131 pertiod of the moneys of the said society so entrusted to him, to his own use and benefi*." The second warrant was by the Wigan Tramways Comp my, that he did " feloniously forge a certain order or request for the payment of the suinof £2OO by endorsing upon a certain cheque for the payment of the said sum to one John Sinith, or order, trcertain mark or cross purporting to be the mark of the said John Smith and signing the same as witness,

EDUCATION COMLITTEE.—The District Education COM- mime reported that during the month of April (live weeks) the numbers of cases before the committee were as follows: —Application for payment of fees, 171; fur contravention of the Education Act, 321. SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTICE.—This committee recomtneud,cl that the resignation of Miss Strickland, head mistress in the senior girls' department ef the Warrington-I road schools be accepted, the engagement to terminate July 31st.--The committee also sub flitted to the Board a new , schedule of salaries of teachers in the Board schools, which, after a short discussion, was approved, as was also the above mentioned recommendation. _

•Holan famous awn THEIR EFFECTS.—Father Finegan, the chairman of 'tlea School Management Committee, said in regard to the questions of Mr. Glover as to home lessons, that the committee lad written to each of the head teachers with a view to prepare themselves to meet and answer Mr. eflover'a inquiry regarding home lessons. Mr. Glover ap- peared to be of opinion that home lessons were or might be injurious to the children. The committee had thought it caurteous to Mr. Glover, and in the interests of the Board to make inquiries, and inquiries were made in the following manlier :—The clerk sent a circular letter to each head teacher in the Board schools asking them their opinion as to whether home lessons were injurious to the health of the children under their charge, and if any co.r plaints had been made by parents against the giving of horde leeeena to that children. He (Father Finegan) had in his hind the letters from each of the bead teachers, and in none of those letters was it stated that home lessons injured the health of any child. Ile believed he was right in saving that in no case had there been any grievance. The teachers as a rule were in favour of home lessons. They had a letter from one master of long experience in which he said that three complaints had been made daring six veers—three applications for remission had been made during six years. He (Father Finegan) consi- dered that was practically nothing. In answer to the Chair- man, Father Finegan said that in each case where a remis- sion of home !engem was asked for by the parent it was I granted by the teach.r.—Mr. Glover asked if the home lessons were considered to be of any value.—Father Finegan aid he assumed from the fact that the teachers set the lessons that they considered them to be of value. In some cases the question had been asked and answered very di- rectly.—Tne Clerk then read letters which bore out Father I penegan's statement, after which the Ch Airman expressed the opinion that Father Finegan tad given answers to Mr. I Glover's questions. It WAS satisfactory, he said, to learn 1 that if parents knew that Wile pressure WAS put upon their children they had their remedy.—Mr. Davies slid that they ought to see that no undu2 pressure Was out upon the pupil teacher. He believed the hours they bad to work ' were very long.—Father Finegan said the teachers had been asked to keep to the time tables as much as possible.—The subject then dropped. - Fireence.—The Finance Committee recommended the payment of the sum of £569 3s 4d. A street disturbance oi-a -ii-o-tn-ew—la-at serious character arose out of an iecident of no importance whatever on Sunday evening in Lngsdale-road. Widnes. Opposite St. Mary's Boman Catholic Church, there is a lodging-house kept by a person named William Jones; and on Sunday evening, about six o'clock, one of the lodgers asked Jones to go to a public house in the locelity and have a drink. Jones had an ob- jection to entering a public house on a Sunday, but a sug- gestion that Mrs. Jones should fetch a pint of beer was acted upon. As she was returning carrying a jug containing the liquor, it is alleged she was stopped by the Bev. Father Clarke, who addressed her on the impropriety of fetching , beer on a:Sunday. With the retort that the priest bad no ' control over her actions, she entered the house, and Father Clarke followed, and addressed to the husband similar vrords to those he bad spoken to the wife. Jones replied that he would brook no interference with his actions by anyone outside, andasked the reverend father to retire. It is stated that Father Clarke declined, and an excited conversation ensued upon Jones threatening to send for a policetnsn to eject him, the upshot being that Father Clarke was pushed into the sired by Jones. The altercation was continued on the parapet, with the natural result that a crowd of about a hundred persons assembled and gave vent to their feelings agiinst Jones by angry shouts and groans. Two constables arriving on the scene, however, partially restored q aietness, but about eight o'clock, when the congregation had left the Catho ic ChurCh, and the policemen had departed, a mob of at least 300 persons assembled round Jones' premises vowing vengeance aiainst the lodging-house keeper for insul- ting the priest. Missiles of various kinds were thrown, and a 0 iosiderable number of panes of glass in the back and front windows were smashed. Inspector Wood with several con- stables proceeded to the spot, and prevented any further display of violence, but the neighbourhood had not resumed its normal condi ion for several henna It is stated that Jones is a member of a local orange lodge, and has aroused the animosity of his Irish neighbours. On Monday even. lug Jones's house was again surrounded by a large crowd of excited people, but the restraining presence of several police officers prevented any outbreak. A case connected with the affair was brought before Mr. John Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday. Michael Carr (17) and John Keenan (15) were charged with stealing 20 cast iron balls, worth 3e 41, the property of the Widnes Foundry Company.— Inspector Wood stated that the balls weighed about a pound each, and were worth twopence a piece. The balls were seen safe at seven o'clock on Sunday morning, and at six o'clock the same evening they were missed. Between seven and eight o'clock the same evening Father Clarke, the parish priest, went to a common londging-house in Lugsdale-road, which was kept by a roan named William Jones. While in the house Father Clarke and Jones bad some unpleasant conversation, which was continued outside. 00 getting ontside a large crowd of people assembled, and they began hissing and hooting and threatening what they would do. The police arrived and disperaed the crowd. About nine o clock the prisoner Carr and several others went to the back of Jones's house, and Carr, who was well known to Jones, threw the bell produced through the back bedroom window of the holm. Jones and his wife were standing in Ith, bedroom looking through the window, and both recog- nised Carr. True ball fell on the bed, and Jones pioked it up. About ten or fifteen minutes afterwards Jones and his wife were standing at the front door, when the prisoner Keenan and a n unifier of others were in the road. Keenan was seen deliberately to throw the second ball produced through the window.—Thomas Wiles, of Sinon's Cross, a labourer at the foundry, and William Jonas. the lodging-house keeper, confirmed this statement, and toe prisoners were remanded. on Wednes• day they were brought before Messrs. G. Pilkington and Holbrook Giskell, Jan, lo compiny with Patrick Devereaux (14) and Michael Kelly (15), who had lasen apprehended in the meantime. Toe only additional °valance was that of P.O Timperley, to whom the prisoners had made statements iucriinin sting each other, it being stated, however, that, Kelly hid a ball given to him by Devereaux. Before decid-; ing thin case, the Bench heard a charge of wilfully damaging Jones' property to the extent of 16s 81 by breaking panes Of glass on dundav evening. In addirion to tne prisoners J.M.I Burns and Jahn McCabe (13) were charged with tin, offence. Mr. liusbind, the deputy colooer, prosecuted. The evidence showed that the prisoners were arrioogd the. crowd ; assembled round J mes' house, and sent museumS which- did tuateratel damage. For the wilful damage, race pi-teener war tined 24 and cests, and ordered to pay a &Liege of the dam age, or io defanß seven days' imprisonment. The Beret dieinissed the charge of rubbery against Kelly, but &tee Devereaux, Keenan, and Carr each 21s, or 14 daye' iin• prison meta.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THLIBSDASI A check is given to-day to the report daily growing. in confidence during the past week that the Gnvornment are actually engaged in preparations for an expedition for the; relief-of- General Gordon. An official communication has been made to the London morning newspapers, which the Ames forlornly reads as fresh proof of the hopeleas wicked- nee, of the Government on this question. I think less , excitable and less prejudiced people will acknowledge that the action of the Government throughout this business has been not only wise but consistent. They have been sub- jected to one of the biggest "put up jobs" in the political ! history of this country. The gallant and simple-minded ; Gordon has been used by the Conservatives with a reckless !disregard both of truth and of the interests of a country of whose honour they proclaim themselves not only chief but sole guardians. He has been picked up and dropped accord- ing to fluctuating circumstances,at one time being a Christian hero deluded and abandoned by a godless Government, at another times more than half mad enthusiast whom an un- intelligent Ministry were permitting to drag them through the mire.

These tamics hay.: been played Rh a coarae recislessnem that as scarcely tried. to bide the clumsiness of its un- reality. What I more paticalarly mean by the "pot up job" is the representation that the whole country cannot sleep at nights for thinking of Gordon and that it spends its days in reviling the Ministry. At least the latter portion of this statement is true as regards that little world known as Clubland and London Society-_a world whome influence is infinitely out of proportion either to its numbers or in- telligence, since in it men who write for the newspapers and men who sit in Parliament chiefly live. But your readers know very well that it is not the case in your town and county, where events are regarded in a different and, I would ven- ture to say, a truer light. Nevertheless, the clamour of London clubs and the chatter of London drawing-rooms incessantly harping on the one theme is always deafening i Ministers, whether heard with tbe ear or read in the columns ' of the Times or other newspapers. It is to the high credit of ministers that they have risen above these rail influences, and have steadily pursued their course. Mr. Ashmead Bartlett's specific demand that a re- lief column should be despatched to Khartoum seven weeks before Gordon set out from London came too late to be seriously considered. The suggestion was, it will be re- membered, only thrown out on debate on the second Vote of Censure. But others differing only in degree, in rank absur- dity and evidence of crassest ignorance for weeks have been clamorously made, chiefly instating upon the immediate despatch of an expedition to die in the desert of thirst aad sunstroke. The answer of the Government to persistent questioning and recurrent votes of censure has been that they hold themselves responsible for the safety of General Gordon. In fulfilment of this pledge, they are now making inquiries as to ways and means and carrying out prelimi- nary preparations, which will enable them when the proper time comes to set the relief column in motion. As there has been no criminal haste neither will there be dangerous delay. Whilst no time will be lost for lack of preparation, the Government are not without hope that, after all, the costly expedition may not be needed, and that Gordon may still do what for weeks he had full opportunity of doing, and deliver himself from Khartoum.

The fair hopes of the Coneervatives, which recently blossomed as the rose, have been suddenly and utterly cast down. This time last week they were rejoicing inasmuch as by the Treaty on the Terrace they had secured the Irish vote, and so nominally reduced the Government majority to 28. It was Lord Randolph Churchill who carried out that negotiation, a reality as opposed to the shadowy com- pact of Kilmainham. The Irish vote was his peace- offering on returning to the Conservative fold. So elated were the Conservatives with this gleam of good fortune that they forthwith determined to throw out the Franchise Bill in the House of Lords. On Tuesday, alas I this plea- sant dream was dissipated. The newly-cemented friend- ships were rudely broken, and Lord It. Churchill, the ablest if not the only able member of the Party, once more went en the rampage. Worse still, he had again parted with his friends on a question on which he was indisputably right, and they were conspicuously wrong. This arose on Lord Claud Hamilton's motion to exclude Ireland from the Franchise Bill, in the division en which the Government majority rose within five of 200. This, lit is admitted in Conservative ranks, is but a poor preparation fer the Lords setting themselves against the popular will. The remarkable hold which the Salvation Army has oh- tainted upon a section of the wealthy public does not ap- pear to be diminished by any recent disclosures. For a time after General Booth's transaction in respect of the Eagle Tavern, subscriptions fell off, and the prosperity of the Army which after all, like the Parnellite faction, is a business community, @bowed signs of decadence. But the Ceeneral has made a new movement. He has entered upon the huntiog grounds of that unquestionably useful body the Blue Ribbon rmy, and has got up a show of reclaimed drunkards much after the fashion of, though a little more disgusting than the show of barmaids or of babies at the Crystal Palace. That he was able, almost at a single meet- ing, .o obtain donations to the amount of £lO,OOO is a fact as great, US to some people it will appear inscrutable. En- couraged by this success the General, who always has a shrewd eye for landed property, has purchased a lease of a piece of ground whose ground rent is £7OO a year, and on this is about to build a mammoth meeting house. At present one of the headquarters of the army on Sun- days is St. James's Hall, Piccadilly. I looked in there the other Sundoy afternoon and if I had not known that it was a religious meeting would have thought it•was a music hall performance. There was on the platform a band of music in which the horn and banjo were prominent instruments. A woman was singing a sofas, a rattling air in whica in due course, the audience joined; whilst the money box was per- sistently going round just as it does about the skims of a crowd assembled to sea street tumblers. The audience was composed largely of servant girls and their young men, who seemed to find the -proceedings sufficiently exciting, the rendezvous convenient, and the seats comfortable.

It is suggested that the watch discovered on Sattuday morning in the room of the Attorney-General at the House of Commons must be that of Mr. Wiggin. A. couple of see- lions ago Mr. Wiggin attempted to fortify himself for the dull round of labours in the House of Commons by a visit to the Aquarium. When he returned he found he had left his water' behind him, and from that day to this it has never been heard of. Some ingenious member has construc- ted out of his inner consciousness a story to the effect that the conscience-stricken thief has come down to the House intending to restore the watch, has sought out the Attorney- General as an appropriate medium for confession and resti- tution, and, his courage failing him at the last moment, secretly dropped the watch on the floor and departed. This is a pretty story, but, unfortunttely, Mr. Wiggin has not been able to identify the watch.

Lord Garmoyle remains an exile. He is making a tour of the world, and means to extend it till the breach of promisa case is disposed of. He is expected at Saratoga when the season opens—rather a dangerous place for a young man of his sosceptibility. The Lord Mayor and Corporation take an active interest in the "City of London Society of Artists and Guildhcli Academy of Art," whose fourth exhibition has just bees opened at the Guildhall. The old law cours have been converted into light and spacious galleries w ere the works displayed can be seen to greater advantage than in the old quarters at skinner's Hall. The scuip:ure is the chief at- traction this'year, through the interest taken by Messrs. Brock, Birch and oiher eminent sculptors, who are repre- sented by some of their best works. The list of painters who exhibit includes Sir F. Leightoiand -malty other. Sir Frederick sends two small heads painted with his usual refinement ; Mr. T. B. Hardy has a fresh ma piece; Mr. W. C. Symons a "Return from the war ;" Mr. H. A peaceful bit of heathy landscape called "A grey day" is by Mr. A. Beleke, and "A ferry on the Thames" by Mr. Tom GI With. Among the contributors of water colour drawings are Mews. Steeple, Alfred Powell, H. S. Marks, C. Ct.ttterraole, and Thomas l'yne.

They believe that if all growers of willows will vigorously pursue the method suggested of catching them that they can this season exterminate them,especially if taken veryelrly before Their progeny are deposited on toe leaf, which will be very shortly, if the hot sunny weather continues, A VILLAGE BOMANCE : UNITED AT Liar:7—A rather romantic wedding took place at Lynam on Monday, when Mr. John Johnson, who is better known in the neighbour- hood under the cognomen of " Trumper," and -Mrs. Mary Holt, of Pepper-street, were united in wedlock at :be old church. The happy couple are by noemeans young, both having passed the half century, and, rather curious to relate, they were engaged in the pleasant occupation of " courting " some forty years ago. It is not difficult to imagine thof dreams of future bliss that they then indulged in, but is their case the old adage of "Many a slip 'twecu the cup and the lip" was once more illivtre•_;:d. From some cause or other the love-making of the pair failed to collie to 's sac- useful termination and they drifted apart. Each in turn found congenial helpmates and entered upon the married state, and now, after such a lapse of time, the lovers, per- haps less enthueiastic though none the less loving than ot yore, have again come together, and thue their •vonthful anticipations have at last been fulfilled. The wedding was attended by a considerable [limber of the relatives of the contracting parties, and after the ceremony the newly- . martitd pair bcl a drive round the neighliAirliond, finishing up with a supper at the Golden F;eece. Mr. and Mrs. John- son are old respected inhabitants of Lymni. and the marriage created considerable interest in the vill3ge.
