EARLESTOWN• BURTONWOOD WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—A scriptural drama ' entitled, "Joseph and his brethren," was given in the Wee. leyan School, Burtonwood, on Saturday evening last by several of the young men connected with the school. Tne characters were well sustained throughout, and the perform- ance was greatly appreciated. At its conclusion a nice programme of song!, recitations, dm., was gone through. A Ronan WIFE AT EARLESTOWN —Oa Monday, at the Newton Town Half, before A. C. McCorquodale, Esq., a married woman named Ellen Banks, residing in Legh-street, Earlestown, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Sankey-street, on Saturday night last.—P.C. Patker stated that he VIW the prisoner drunk in Sankey-street, and she was creating a great disturbance. She beat h r husband, and behaved in a violent manner towards other persons who passed her. The constable tried to get the woman quiet, but he was at last compelled to lock her up.—She was committed to prison for seven days. CO-OPERATIVE STORES EMPLOYES. —On Wednesday evening a meeting was held of the employes of the Earles- town Co-operative Society, 17 in number, who after discus- sing business matters adjourned to the Welcome Coffee Palace, IHarket-place, where after partaking of some refresh- ments several songs and recitations were given. Master Ben Tripp played several pieces on his violin. During the evening Mr. Jackson gave an original song in excellent style, composing the verses as he sang. A social and pleasant eveaing was spent. A VIOLENT MAN AT THE RAILWAY STATION —On Satur- day, at the Newton Town Hall, before T. J. Gillespie, Esq., Patrick Cunningham was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Earlestown, on the previous evening.—From the statement of P.S. Commins it appeared that the prisoner was very druek on Earlestown station, and was pat off the platform by Benjamin Higson, night porter. The prisoner went away, but returned in a short time, and Higson again requested him to leave. He refused to do so, and imme- diately struck Higson in the face. He was eventually put outside the station, and as P.S. Commins and two cmstables were in the vicinity at the time, and heard the prisoner using violent and indecent language, they took him into custody.—He was fined lOs and costs. SAD CASE OF WIFE DESERTION AT EARLESTOWN.—A sad case of desertion of a wife and child came before Mr. T. J. Gillespie, at the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday afternoon last, when Richard Read, a collier lately residing at Newton Common, was charged with having deserted his wife and child on the 3rd Octouer last.—Frorn the statement of P.S. Commins it appeared that the circumstances of the case were of a sad and painful character. The prisoner Was a collier in good employment previous to the 3rd October last, on which date he suddenly deserted his wife and cbild, the wife being then ill. The relieving officer (Mr. Caldwell) supplied her not only with maintenance, but also with medical attendance, but she ultimately died.—The prisoner was remanded to the Petiy Sessions at Warrington, where he was brought up on Wednesday, and committed to prison for six weeks. LORD JUSTICE CAVE AND LORD JUSTICE DAY AT NEWTON. —Newton was honoured on Saturday last by the prssence of the well-known Lord Justice Cave and Lord Justice Day, who have been conducting the recent assizes at Liverpool. They visited Newton as the guests of Colonel George Mc- Corquodale, J.P., by whom they were entertained; among the gentlemen and friends present being the Rev. 11. Monk (vicar of Newton),. the Rev Father F. J. Lennon, &c. On the following day Lord Justice Day accompanied Colonel McCorquodale to divine service in St. Peter's Church, where the Rev. H. Monk was the preacher; while Lord Justice Cave attended the Catholic Church in Craw-lane, where service was conducted by the Rev. Father Lennon. The presence of these gentlemen created some interest and conversation in the village on Sunday. They returned to Liverpool on Monday. NARROW ESCAPE OF A CHILD ON THE RAILWAY.— STOPPING •AN EXPRESS Talate—A little girl named Roberts, daughter of Henry &bens, residing in a row of cottages neat the Vulcan Iron Foundry, Earlestown, had an extraordiearir escape of being cut to pieces by an express train on the railway, on Thursday afternoon. It appears tint the child was playing with a number of other children on a plot of land near the level crossing at the Vulcan, and unobserved wandered on to the lines. As the express train due from Warrington at 12-50. far Newton Bridge and Man- chester was approaching, the pointsrnan in the Vulcaa sig- nal box (Richard Croft) observed the danger threatening the child, and at once threw up the signal against the ap• proaching train, and attracted the attention of the driver by pointing to the child in front. The driver quickly stint off steam and made an effort to bring the train to a standstill, but the child, unconscious of the danger to which it was ex- poried, stood admiring the approaching express with evident pleasure and admiration. 'the driver, however, succeeded in bringing the train to a standstill, the infant then being but two or three yards in front. The child was quickly re• moved, and the train proceeded on its journey. As the Vulcan Ironworks had just stopped for the dinner hour the incident created considerable excitement, and the narrow escape of the child was much talked ahead in the after- noon.

IHR LANCASHIRE HUSSARS YEOMANRY CAVALRY AT SODTHPORT.—Tae Lancashire Hussars Yeomanry Cavalry, composed of the A (Aehton-in-Makerfield), B (St. Helens and Wigan), C (Newton and Liverpool), and D (Ormskirk I and Liverpool) troops concluded their annual week's special training at Southport on Wednesday last. The regiment arrived at Southport on the previous Wednesday, and have been commanded by Major the Right Hoe. the Earl of Lathom, in the absence of Colonel W. J. Legh, M.P., Ma sick leave. Taken on the whole the weather was of a very favourable character, the only real drawback being the somewhat heavy downpour on the Thursday. On Friday afternoon the horses were paraded for inspection and the , award of prizes, the judges being the commanding officer and Major Earle, assisted by veterinary-surgeon Dixon. In the A (Ashton) troop the prime, were awarded —lst, Corporal Robert Turner; 2nd, Sergeant Straw; 3rd, Corporal Tom Pendlebary. B (St. Helens and Wigan) troop-Ist, Private Ashcroft; 2nd, Pri- vate William Alker ; 3rd, Corporal Critchley. C (Newton) troop: Ist, Lance-Corporal W. Hope ; 2ad, Corporal S. Pimblett ; 3rd, Farrier4ergeant Ritchie. D (Ormskirk) troop: Ist, Private Fletcher ; 2nd, Private Birchall ; 3rd, Corporal Langdon. The regimental horse prize was won by Corporal Robert Turner (Ashton-in- Makerfleld). On Saturday the sword exercise competition was held, and so creditable were the performances that the judge (Troop-Sergeant-Major Pinnell, of the 11th Hussars, Liverpool) declared their achievements made I them, on the average, quite as competent swords- ; men as men in regiments of the line. The , prize winners were—" A" troop: Sergeant James I Glover, let ; Farrier Sergeant Thomas Pilling, 2nd; Pri- vate George Heath, 3rd. "B " troop: Corporal Joshua i Sumner, lot; Private W Critchley, senior, 2nd; Private Joseph Horridge, 3rd. "C,, troop : Quarter-master ser- geant-major T Howard, let; Private Robert Ritchie, 2nd ; Private M Holgate,' 3rd. "D " troop: Corporal Spencer, 1 Ist; Private Cave, 2nd; Private Lipscombe, 3rd. The re- gimental prize was won by Quarter-master-sergeant T , Howard. The church parade took place on the I Sunday, and on the following day the sketch- ing competition was held ; the regimetital prizes being obtained by Quarter - Master Sergeant - Major Livesley (Ashton) Ist, and Private Pennington (Newton) 2nd. The annual review of the regiment was held by Lord R. De Kerr, on Tuesday afternoon, who, after one of the 1 best reviews ever held in Southport, highly commended the men on their evolutions, and expressed his admiration of the 'manner in which every officer and man appeared eager to maintain the high character for efficiency which had always been held by the Lancashire Hussars. The regiment left Southport on Wednesday last, the return of the various troops creating considerable interest in the towns to which 11 they belonged. 1 AN EARLESTOWN CASE AT LIVEEPOOL Assimms: CLAIM 1 AGAINST THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.—Before Mr. Justice Cave and a special jury, at ' the Liverpool Assizes, on Saturday last, Mrs. Egan, a widow, sued the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany and John Elliott, for damages on account of injury caused to the furniture of a house occupied by her in Crown- street, in November, 180. The railway company paid £lO Into court, but denied the negligence. Dr. Commins (instruc- ted by Mr. F. Murphy) was for the plaintiff; Mr Gully and Mr. Ernest Page (instructed by Mr. C. H. Mason) represen- ted the railway company; and Mr. Walton (instructed by Messrs. R. Davies and Co.) appeared for the defendant Elliott. The railway company towatdarthe close of the year 1830 engaged the defendant Elliott, who is a contractor, carrying on business at Earlestown, to pull down for rail- way improvements certain houses in Crown-street, adjoining that occupied by the plaintiff, and the case of the plaintiff was that the work was negligenty and carelessly performed, 30 as to cause serious injury to the gutter and rain pipes of her house, in consequence of which a quantity of water forced its way into the building, and did great damage to the furniture. The plaintiff became ill owing to the damp- ness of the house, ant lost two lodgers, and assessed the damage at £250. Mrs. Egan stated that she had applied several times to the railway company for settlement of her claim, but they had put her off, and only offered her £5. Before the conclusion of the plaintiff's case, his Lordship observed that it was shocking for a railway company to bring such a cause into court. The matter might have been settled in about a fortnight after it occurred if it had been gone into properly —Mr. Gully said that endeavours had been made to Bettie it.—His Lordship rejoined that the plaintiff did not go to her solleitor until May last year. It was a frightful waste of the company's money, as the case might have been settled for a tenth part of the law costs.— Mr. Gully said that the plaintiff would not accept a reason- able offer —His Lordship replied that so far there had been no evidence of that, lost the company could not call £5 a reasonable offer. The time of special juries ought to be taken up only in trying commercial cases, as they had their own business to attend to.—Mr. Gully alter a brief consul- tation with the representatives of the railway company, said he was prepared, as far as the company was concerned, to assent to a verdict, which Dr. Coalmine agreed to. Re did so, feeling it would be useless to ga on with the case after a d asked wd what his lordship had said. He did not gay he could so have altered the facts to the extent of showing that the rail- waythit companythe claim n nog wone.—Hi d . ti Lordship itpo Mr. Walton what course he intended to pursue, and said that if he succeeded in getting a verdict in his favour his aetxag liable, era t client would have to pay his own costs. The case never ought to have come into court. Very likely the claim was an exaggerated one, owing to the time that bad elapsed, but it ought to have been met in a proper spirit at the time, and settled. A juryman was then withdrawn as regarded the iefendant Elliott, and a verdict by consent for £4O, inclu- ding the £lO paid late court, given against the railway company With coats.

SHOCKING ACCIDNNT TO A LAD.—OH Thursday afternoon a lad n oiled James HiII, sen of Mr. Hill, clogger, Markel- street, Earlestown, met with a serious accident in the goods station yard, belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Company. The lad was playing about the " crane" in the yard, and, it is stated, climbed up tte chain. In descending he 8:1d down too rapidly, and the large iron book at the bottom of the chain caught between his legs, and caused a deep gash in the flesh, which was also much torn. roe poor lad was very seriously injured, and after being removed home medical attendance was called in.

FAIR AT NSWTON.—What is known as the "May fair" was held at Newton on Saturday, and as the weather was very fine, with a powerful sun overhead, the usually quiet village presented a very busy and animated appearance from early in the morning to late at night. In the earlier part of the day the annual horse, cattle, and pig sale was held, and was of a very successful character, considering the Local Government restrictions upon the cattle trade, in con- sequence of the existence of foot and mouth disease, which have only recently been withdrawn. There were over 200 head of cattle a-id about 300 horses offered for sale, and the attendance of buyers from Manchester, Liverpool, and other towns was unusually large. The cattle were of an average Quality, and many were sold, while the horses, which were on the whole far superior to the average quality, were some- what rapidly disposed of. A fair trade was also done in the pig business. In the afternoon and evening a number of swings, gingerbread, and sweet stalls and other attractions drew some hundreds of persons from the neighbouring country, who appeared to heartily enjoy themselves. The charmingly situated Newton Lake also formed an attraction, and many persons enjoyed a row upon it, or a ramble in its vicinity.

MINERS' MEETING AT HAVDOCE —A meeting of miners was held in a field behind the Waggon and Horses, at Haydock, on Tuesday, at which Mr. Woods, of Park-lane, Haydock, gave an address on questions affecting the working classes both locally and generally. He pointed out to them the benefits that accrued from the Miners' Federation, and exhorted all present to work unitedly and harmoniously together. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL.-00 Sunday last two sermons were preached in the above chapel, after- noon and evening, by the Rev. R. Crewdson, of Golborne. In the morning a service of Song, entitled "The Passage of the Red Sea," was rendered by the Primitive Methodist choir of Parr; a selection of pieces was given by the chil- dren and also by the choir, uneler the leadership of Mr. H. I Harrison. Mr. J. Livesley, jun., occupied his urinal posi- tion at the organ. Ths collections amounted to £6 3s. 11d., being about the amount of last year. A HAYDOCK. MAN DROWNED AT ST. HELENS.—Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest on Monday, at the Prin- cess Royal Inn, Park-road, on the body of John Down, a collier, formerly living with his brother at Haydock, who was found drowned in the Sankey Canal, belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Company, near the Redgate Bridge, Parr, on Saturday morning last —Mr. For- rand (Liverpool) watched the case on behalf of the railway company.—Michael Dowd, miner, Haydock, id.ntified the deceased as his brother, and said he was a miner 38 years of age. He lived with witness, who last saw him alive be- tween twelve and one o'clock on Saturday, the 3rd instant, when, after getting his dinner, he said be was going out for a walk. He was of a cheerful disposition, and always read his daily paper. There was nothing whatever to lead to the supposition that he would make away with himself. When witness last saw him he was perfectly sober.— In reply to a juror, witness said deceased might have been to St. Helens and come back along the canal, when he fell or walked in. He could not say whether he could swim. He sometimes indulged in a little drink on a Saturday Phillip Fogarty, of Park-road, Parr, deposed to finding the body of the deceased in the canal between six and seven o'clock on Saturday morning, near the bridge, and about 10 yards from a barge moored in that part of the canal. The body was lying nearly opposite the barge, and on dragging it out he sent word to the police. Witness recollected Jas. Develin being drowned there about the same place, where OD the bank there was a bar or rail which was occasionally lifted in order to load or discharge the barges.—P.C. JAITI`qt Ratcliffe stated that he attended the inquest en the 26th • December, 1882, on the body of James Develin, who was found near the same place where Dowd' s body was found. There was a loose bar there which was lifted in and out of a socket when occasion required. The jury then made a presentment that the moveable bar should have a better clamp, so as to make the rail more secure. It was lees secure now than it was then, nothing having been done to carry into practical effect the presentment that the jury then made. The inquest on Develin was held before Mr. Barker, the late coroner. The depth of the water at that point then, as now, was seven feet, and there was a drop of about nine feet from the bank to the surface.— The Coroner said he was somewhat astonished that the pre- sentment of the jury on the occasion of the last inquest at the same place should not have been carried out. It so happened that the deceased's body wart' found near the same spot where the poor fellow Develin was found drowning some time ago, and although they had no evidence that the rail was down on either occasion, there was a strong pre- sumption that it was.—The foreman of the, jury remarked that the Isar catch was now in a worse state than when the presentment was made before the late Mr. Barker, nothing whatever having been done to it.—The jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned," and added a presentment that the clamp of the protection rail or bar on the bank of the canal at that particular spot should be properly repaired and made secure by tlre Railway Company.

div.head: DISPUTE AT ST. JOHN'S CHURCH.
div.p: THE DISPUTE AT ST. JOHN'S CHURCH.

Judging from present appearances, the squabble at St. John's Church, Earlostown, which has given that place of worship an unenviable notoriety throughout the cauntry, seems to have been at last settled. Whether or not the "old sore" will be re-opened time alone will tell, but the ser- vices on Sunday last were as orderly, peaceful, and hearty as anyone could possibly have wished. Both morning and evening the members of the choir were in their accustomed places ; Mr. H. J. Darman presided at the organ ; the vicar and curate gave out hymns, which the choir and congrega- tion sang; and the prayers, psalms, &c., were heartily re- sponded to. The sermons by the curate, the Rev. H. E. Smith (in the morning), and the vicar, the Rev. T. R. Mat- thews (in the evening), were attentively listened to by large congregations. The usual offertories were also taken ; though the amount collected, we are informed, was much below the average of former days. It is to be hoped that the last of the unseemly squabbles and disturbances has been witnessed.

LIBERALISM AT EARLESTOWN. LECTURE ON FOREIGN AND FINANCIAL feCESTIONS. On Tuesday evening a public meeting was held to the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, Earlestown, under the aus- pices of the Earlestown and District Liberal Club, and the Rev. J. D. Alford, representing the Financial itefot.m Association, delivered a lecture entitled "The Foreign and Financial Policy of the Government." No doubt the beautifully fine weather influenced the attendance to a cer- tain extent, but notwithstanding there was a large audience, among those present, in addition to the lecturer, being Messrs. M. Birkhead (who presided), J. Ball, E. Haworth, P. Thompson, John Clarke, T. Howard (secretary), &c. The Chairman' in opening the meeting, read a corn- rnunicaion from Mr.. Charles Pilkington, J.P. (vice-presi- dent of the club), who explained his inability to attend. He went on to-say that he (the chairman) was a Liberal and a thorough Radical, and he had been so ever since be knew anything at all about politics, because he was reared in an agricultural district where the parson and squire were sup- reme, and where workingmen had not the advantages they had in the present day. Theythen had no power either one way or another. Since that time his-inclinations had been on the side of Liberalism, and the more he looked upon what had been, done by Liberals the more convinced he was that Liberalism was the thing they had to fight for and stand by. He maintained that anything and everything which had been done to elevate the working classes had been dune by Liberals; road everything that had had for its object the intellectual or temporal, or moral elevation of the working classes had been fought against by the " squire- ocracy of the land, and therefore he (the chairman) was a thorough-going Literal, and as far as he possibly could be would back up the-present Government or any other Gov- ernment that was going in the same track. (Loud applause.) The present Government were harassed in many ways, and the Tories were doing all they could to obstruct and retard the progress of the Franchise Bill which they as Liberals were anxious to see. (Applause.) The ,Tories did not care so much about the Egyptian question as they were anxious to keep back the tide of Reform, and if they could keep back the Franchise Bill so long that it could not be passed they would only be well pleased what might become of General Gordon. (Applause.) He then introduced Mr. Alford.

The Lecturer was warmly received. He remarked that he was like the chairman, a Radical, and he prided himself that he was a Radical. Referring to the statement of the chairman at a recent Conservative gathering in that hall, he (the lecturer) said he did not see that the present Govern- ment was endangering the interests of the country, as Mr. Westhead appeared to think. He (Mr. Westhead), had stated that Mr. Gladstone was ashamed of the whole Egyp- tian business, and was anxious to wipe out the recollection of it from the minds of the people; and he further said that the Liberal party were trying to prevent a discussion upon the Egyptian question. There could be no doubt Mr. Glad- stone was ashamed of the whole Egyptian business, and was anxious to wipe his hands clean of it; but the Tories wanted to talk about Egypt and nothing else. They wanted to talk from morning till night, from Monday to Saturday, and, be- cause the Government says "No, we have some practical business to attend to, and we will and must attend to it," and because one of the matters which the Government, in- sisted upon giving to the people the Franchise Bill they turned round and said that the Government wanted to evade a discussion. The Tories were anxious to talk about the Egyptian question, but did not like the votes upon it— (hear, hear,)—and because the Government insisted upon a discussion of other pressing matters they said that the Government was destroying freedom of speech. He man- ta Med that the Liberals of the present day were fighting for the same principle as Cobden and the Liberals of his day; andytated that he thought the policy of the Government in insisting upon the Soudan being given up was a perfectly wise policy, but how to get the garrisons out was another question. General Gordon was sent there for two or three objects—he was sent to bring the garrisons out if he could, was sent there to establish a Government if he could, but it was very clear that he was sent there not to establish, an English Government—(hear,. hear,)—but to establish a Government of the natives, and yet the Tories wanted to make out that tlie Government had assumed the government of the Soudan, and that they were responsible for the con- dition and circumstances of the garrisons. He proceeded to allude to the franchise question, remarking that it was a contest between the aristocracy and the democracy, and a question of equal rights and liberties. The great ques- tion was whether the House of Commons should be a House representing the opinions of a few men or whether it should be a House constituted by the whole people. The House of Commons as it at present existed, was not constituted by the whole people, and the Liberal party were very anxious to bring about such a change so that the House should re- present the whole people. (Applause.) The Tories', how- ever, wished to divert the attention of the people from that franchise bill by turning to the question of Egypt. The franchise question involved the life or death of the Tory party and they knew it, and consequently they were anxious to put it aside, frustrate, and if possible destroy the fran- chise question—a question to them of life and death. He maintained that the last Tory government was elected by a minority of the electors of he country, and stated that an extension of the franchise would result in a great gain to the Liberal party. So long as any number of people were un- enfranchised they could not get the real sentiment of the country; and there were immense masses of the population —most of them Liberals—who could not at present exercise the privilege of a vote. Remarking that he would like to say a word or two upon the question of finance, he said lee was anxious to do it as the reptesentative of the Financial Reform Association. He maintained that the Dreaent govern- ment had been compelled to increase the taxation of the country in order to pay off the debts and legacies of their predecessors, and yet the Tories were going about the coun- try, and he (the lecturer) thought it was mean and contemptible on their part, pointing to that large increase on the expenditure of the country. He pointed out that the Financial Reform Associ- ation was founded for the purpose of securing economical Government, just taxation, and perfect freedom of trade. Many evils remained in the shape of taxes on trade; for whenever they put a tax on, trade they embarrassed trade. encumbered it, and made it difficult; but not only did they embarrass trade and make it difficult but they intro:zinced inequalities in the taxation. He wished to know lithe working men of the country, with the knowledge of those facts before them would allow the present system of taxa- tion to continue when they once obtained power in the House ef Commons. ("No.") They need not wonder at Lord Salisbury and the Tory party moving earth, and not heaven, but the other place, for the purpose of obstructing the Franchise Bill; and putting forth all the powers they could, good, bad, and indifferent almost, for the purpose of preventing the bill becoming law. They had personal in- terests involved in the question, but once let the people I have a mastery in the House of Commons, and sooner or I later they would have a system of taxation far more just than the present one. (Applause.) In concluding he main- 1 tained that if the Egyptian question must be dealt with there was no reason why the Franchise Bill should be pushed aside. Let them go in for the Franchise Bill and support the Government with all their heart and the utmost of their power until that bill became law. (Loud ap- plause.) Mr. John Ball moved, Mr. Thomas Howard seconded, a vote of thanks to the Lecturer which was heartily accorded, and after a similar compliment had been paid to the Chair- man, the meeting concluded.

THE WicaN COIL TRADE.—The depressed state of the coal trade ha led the Ince Hall Coal and Cannel Company, Wigan' to decide upon voluntary liquidation. Work was brought to a close on Thursday. The company have em- plow-d between 800 and 1,000 men. An action has been brought ender the Crimea Act by the two sons of John Joyce, who was murdered with other mem• Oars of his family at Maamtratina. to recover compensation to the amount of £4,000. Evidence was given with great reluctance by some of tbe approvers and others concerned indirectly in the massacre, and the evidence will be laid before the Lord Lieutenant.

S. HELENS. CHARGE 01 ASSAULT AGAINST t SCHOOLICASTEN.,--AI the St. Helens Town 1141 on Monday last, before Mr. A. ATTEMPTED GETTEACIE.—At the St. Helens Town 12a11, on Monday, before A. Sinclair, RNA, and Alderman Mcßryde, Joseph McMullen, a young man, was charged with indeeent ' conduct tOwards Mary McMahon, a widow, residing at I', Store-street, Parr.—The evidence showed that the prisoner lived in the street named, and on the night of the previone Friday he entered the house of the proeecutrix, and while she was in bed attempted to commit an indecent assaalCr upon her. She screamed and several neighbours came in, whereupon the prisoner ran away.—He had nothing to say, and was committed for trial at the next Quarter Sessions. I ALLEGED USII OF • GUN WITHOUT A LICENSE.—At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Mrnday, Henry Leather, of Yew Tree Farm, near Bold, for whom Mr. W. Swift appeared, was summoned by the Supervisor of Inland Revenue for having in his pesseasion and using a gun without having a linense entitling him to do so. It appeared that on Sunday night, the 13th ult., police-constable 203 saw the defendant come from the back of his house on to the road leading into some fields, when he shouldered a gun and fired. Defendant then returned to the house by the back way. Witness went to the front window, which had neither blinds nor shutters, and saw the defendant come into the house by the back door, carrying a single barreled gun.and followed by a neighbour. Defendant then went to a chest of draws and took from one of its compartments a powder flask, from which he com- menced re-loading the gun. The constable thereupon knocked at the door and was admitted. In reply to the question as to whether he had a gun license, defendant said he had not, and taking down another gun, an old rusty one, from the wall, said that was the only gun he had to shoot with. The officer, however, knew better, and told him so.— As che subsequent evidence was very contradictory, the case was dismissed.

PREPARING A DISEASED COW FOR FOOD AT Sr. HELENS. —On Monday a butcher named Robert Metcalf was charged by the St. Helens Corporation, under the 116th section of the Public Health Act, with having deposited in a slaughter- house the carcase of a beast which Was diseased, and which when found was in course of preparation for the food of man.—Mr. Walter Swift prosecuted, and Mr. R. W. H. Thomas defended.—Mr. Swift said that the facts of the case were very simple. A milk-dealer named Fletcher, living at Parr, had a cow which was diseased, and he wanted to get rid of it. He went down to the shambles on the 3rd May and met defendant, to whom he agreed to sell the beast for £3.- On Sunday morning Metcalf took the cow away to a slaughter-house in Tontine-street, and as he was driving it down Park-road at a rapid rate he was noticed by PS- lons and P.C. Carruthers. Ross followed him, and when he reached the slaughter-house he found defendant and a maw named Pemberton dressing the carcase. Inspector Coughtrey soon afterwards examined the meat and found it was diseased, and on his representation and the Medical Officer of Health's certificate it was destroyed.—ln cross- examination Fletcher, the owner of the cow, said a veteri- nary surgeon had told him the cow's heart had slipped, and fearing it might die suddenly, as it was in-calf, and that it might become useless to him he sold it. It was in fair con- dition. The slipping of the heart would not injure the quality of the meat —ln answer to Mr. Sinclair, witness said he gave £2O for it, and if it bad been in perfect condi- tion it would have been worth £2O to sell again. He asked defendant £4, but sold it him for M.—Mr. Coughtrey, the inspector, said the carcase was diseased. He had never heard of such a complaint as the dropping of the cow's heart.—Dr. McNicoll said tbe .carcase was that of a beast which had been diseased before death.—For the defence Mr. Thomas said the carcase will not intended for food. De- fendant bad bought it for such purpose, bet finding it dis- eased he did not intend to sell it for food.—The magistrates inflicted a fine of £5 and 19s costs.

01 A Rem MAU eon NSEQUENCES.—Before . 1 -- Mr. A. Sinclair and Alderman Mcßryde, at the St. Helens Town Hall, en Monday, Stephen Ramsey, an elderly man, was summoned for assaulting hie-wife Ellen, on the 7th inst.—Mr. W. Swift represented the complainant, and stated that the parties had only been married a short time, but on the date named he came home drunk, smashed some of the furniture, knocked the crockery about, turned his stepson , out of the house, and assaulted his wife. Since then the latter had been living apart from him—Ellen Ramsey, wife of the defendant, stated that she lived at 146, Robins-lane, and she was married to the defendant on the 6th March last. On the 7th inst, he came home drunk, and used very bad language. He threatened to knock her head off, and had threatened to take her life many times. He upset_tbe_toble„ smashed some furniture, and struck her. He took up a lamp and held it over her, whereupon she screamed ;and he put her and her son out of the house. She dare not live with him, and had not since been near him. He had assaulted her many times before that.—The defen- dant stated that there had been some difference between them with regard to money matters, which had been th 6 cause of all the trouble. They were married very quickly —they were perfect strangers almost. They were both in rather poor circumstances, the fact being that they borrowed a little money to get married with. The money had to be paid back lust as they could manage, but because he had really been unable to pay on account of the expenses going on in his house, and had tried to keep the expenses down, the whole of the fat was in the 6re, and they had bad a lot of unpleasant circumstances. He had been frequently annoyed, and on the date in question he was excited because several persons with whom he offered to be friends refused his friendship. In the excitement be upset the table, and the lamp fell. He did not intend to assault her, and his wife knew different. He was all love and respect for her, and did not intend to hurt a hair of leer head. These were the circumstances that had brought that hit of family quarrel about. He thought if they bad been left to themselves and others not interfered, the matter would have been settled.— The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO and one surety of £5 ST. HELENS LIBRARY COIdISITTER: MONTHLY MBETING. —The monthly meeting of the Library Committee was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday afternoon' when there were present: Mr. H. R. Lacey (in the chair), Councillors Han- son and R. G. Brook, Dr. McNicoll, and Messrs. A. Sinclair, J.P., N. Lacey, A. Lancister (librarian), and J. H. Craike (deputy town clerk.) The minutes of the last meeting were, read and confirmed.—Librariaa's Report : The monthly re- port of the librarian (Mr. A. Lancaster) showed that the number of books borrowed from the lending library during the month of April was 5.435, an increase on the correspon- ding month of last year of 643; borrowed from the refer- ence department 387, increase 164. The number of guarantee forms received was 39, for which cards had been issued. The cash received during the same period amounted to £2 Uts op, as follows: Fines for undue atten- tion of books £2 55., sale of catalogues 6s 7d, sundries 7s 10. Presents of the following books bad been made: "County. Franchise and Liberal Policy," by Sir Thomas Dyke Ackland. by the author; large map of the Dominion of Canada (10ft. 2M. by Sit. 3in ), by the High Commis- sioner for Canada; official hand-book .of the Dominion of Canada (two copies), by the Canadian High Commissioner; "Cuthbert of Lindisfarne, hi a life and times," by Alfred C. Fryer (two copies), by the author: seven pamphlets, by the Liberty and Property Defence League ; Ninety-third re- port of the Stirling and Glasgow Public Library, by the committee; "Modern Progress in Mine Engineering." by Henry Bramwell, Liverpool, by the author; Report on the Mitchell Library. Glasgow, far 1883, by the committee; "Strictures on Religious Creeds and Usages," by John Earp, by the author; Report of the Birmingham Library (1883), by the committee; Life of Sir Anthony Panizai, K.C.8., by Louis Fagan, two vols., by Mr. Sinclair; First , Annual Report of the Ealing Free Public Library, by the committee. During the month the number of attendances on Sundays was 547, the average being 136 7 ; and last year 581, average 112,2. The report was passed as read.—The Proposed New Library: Councillor Brook asked if the Parliamentary Committee had taken any action with regard to the recommendation of the Library Committee to erect a new public library.—The Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. Crake) replied that at the last meeting of the Parliamentary Com- mittee there was so much business that the question of a new public library was not reached. It would, however, be discussed at a meeting of the Parliamentary Committee to be held that afternoon.—Thie was the only business of in- terested

The de. ; fence was that plaintiff's engagement eras conditional upon , another man sot returning to his work.—after a little eon-, versatioa between His Honour, Mr. Swift, and the plaintiffo His Honour gave a verdict for the plaintiff for 10:r. with costs.--John Gott, also a baker, sued Peter Wright. a grocer and baker in Liverpool-road, St. Helen, for the saw of Ll 18s., alleged te be due as a week's wages in lien of notice.—Mr. Riley appeared for the defence.—The plaintiff alleged that be was summarily dismissed Without sufficient reason on Good Friday last, and claimed the amount named in lieu of a week's notice.—For the defence, it was main- tained that the plaintiff came to his wok at half-past nine at night under the induencs of drink—too, drunk to cic, any- thing. Ihe defendant accordingly dismissed him at once. whereupon the plaintiff became abusive, used bad language, and refused to leave the premises until e polif:eman was sent for.—His Honour believed the account of the defendant that the plaintiff was negligent and drunk, and stated that he did not think the plaintiff war entitled to the week's wages. He, however, gave a verdict for the plaintiff for es.; one day's wages which the defendant had stopped because be had no work for the plaintiff to do.

ST. HELENS PAVING- COMMITTEE DEPUTATION FROM LORD GERARD. The monthly meeting of this committee was .held 08 Wednesday afternoon, at the Town Hall, St. Helene. Alder- man Johnson presided, and there were also present--eCuun- eillors Beletier, Hanson, Fisher, Longton, and Foster ; M.r. Craik (deputy town clerk), and Mr. Gaskin (engineer): het the last meetiog Mr. F. J. Brown attended, and urged the committee to recommend the Conecil to rescind an crder calling upon property owners to complete certain streets. Mr. Brown specially referred to Wrell-street, in whick he has property. His contention was thareit was high and &Ye in fair condition, and not a maid road ; and that it would be a hardship upon him and upon other owners in parallel cases. The committee decided to visit each of the streette named in the order, and, having done so; decided not to re", commend any alteration in the existing order of the Conn' cll. Between the rneetings of the commiette a comnannica-' tion had beeen received from the agent of Lord Gerard, re" ,specting the completion of certain streets oa that portion a . his lordship' estate which lies between College-street, Gerard's Bridge, and the Town Hall. On WednesdaY, *de- putation, consisting of Mr. Moubert (agent to Lord Gerard), , Mr. Walmsley (Solicitor), and Mr. lioldsworth (surveyor), waited upon the committee. Mr. Walmsley said, in the or instance, he would state the circumstances under which the 5 deputation attended that day. The Corporatien had tent notices to sewer, level, pave, and otherwise complete certain 04 streets within the borough. The greater portion q-- Frederick-street, and certain portions of Tolver, Clifton, Cauafield-streets were all on land which was either owneu by Lord Gerard. or which he was interested in through his lessees. He (Mr. Walrnalea ) might say at once that no ene could be more willing than Lord Gerard was to melte any outlay which would improve the sanitary eondition .of his' property, but at the same Owe he was not willing to spend money in making improvements and alterations which might be unneceeeaul and unprofitable; and his lordship was advised that certain of these works that had been, ordered by the Corporation were at the present moment unnecessary and undesirable. He was sure the Corporation would meet them in a friend!! spirit.—Mr. Geldsworth said the deputation would not have gone there that day if it had been simply a question of mini' , tary improvement. So far as sewering an I draining Wes concerned, he thought Mr. Moubert was quite at one with the committee that it required to be done, and therefore it was simply a question of paving. They agreed that the small street should be completed, but as regarded Frederiek- , street, on one side of which not a single house had beeri erected, they asked that they' might do it piecemeal, say the digging flagging first, and call upon owners as buildings proceedeu to kerb, and channel it at a future time. In reply to the Chairman as te what Mr. Goldsworth proposed the 'Corper- . ation should do, the latter replied that in the carrying of new streets to completion. it 'seemed to him desirable to haV. i classification. The specifications. which the Corporation caused the streets to be done by were the same for all sorts of streets. That was to say that Church-street, which had the greatest traffic in the town, Was under the same rule as 1%114 the Corporation had for saeets where the traffic was Volt light indeed. , DANGEROUS EMPLOYMENT IN CHEMICAL WORKS. RBOOMMENDATION EY A, JURY. An inquest on the body of Job Edam, a fitter at Green- bank Chemical Works, wha met with his death under shocking circumstances, was held at the Running Bore' Inn, St. Helens, on Monday forenoon, before Mr. S. Brig" house, coroner. The following evidence was adduced :-- •Elizabeth Erlam said thedeceased was her husband, on._,d be 1?: was a fitter at Greenbank Chemical Works. They reeitl; Canal Bank West-street. Her husband was 34 Years On the 3rd instant be came home from bin work. 7),. not change his clothes, as he expected that be w°6l" "a" to return to his work. He was /mated in the kitchen bef,re the fire, arid struck a match to light his. pipe. He was with- out his coat, and a spark fell from his pipe upon his waist' r coat. It immediately burst into a flame; and itness,. screamed. The next door neighbour came in and ex- , tinguished the flames. A doctor was afterwards sent for,, w and attended the deceased up to the tima of his death on, , Saturday afternoon. The deceased had been working at the Greenbank Chemical Works for about 18 months; and for about a fortnight past he had been employed in the depart- , ment where they made the chlorate. All the other hands employed therein had special clothes made to put on while, at work, but deceased had not, as he was only temporarliY there. Deceased bad been told by neighbours that it woe , very dangerous for him not to change his clothes. The company provided special suits of clothes for the men to wear. Witness had never heard her husband complain that the company would not let him have a suit of clothes. See did not know whether her husband had asked for a suits of clothes..—Richard Isherwood, enginter and manager at ,Greenbank Alkali Works, deposed that he knew the de:, 'eeased, who was a fitter at the works. About the 3rd instant the proprietors were trying a sort of experiment in th chlorate grinding department, and the deceased wae eeT there with a number of other fitters. They were only worn' lug there temporarily; but the chlorate grinder who tow there regularly had a special suit of clothes. As the del, ceased was only temporarily therein he was not found OE clothes, but was cautioned to brush the chlorate off , clothes when leaving the room.—The Coroner: This shows that the fitter runs as much risk as the chlorate grinder, and yet you only find one man a suit of clothe" , Mr. Isherwood: Yes, but we caution them of the danger et: tending the material, and to take care to bruah it all ou their clothes. The deceased was not the only fitter work: • ing there at the time.—The Coroner : If be was a fitter ale° not a chlorate grinder be would not have the same intimate knowledge of the dangereus material as the man who leed„ grinding it.—Mr. Isherwood: The thing is we" known throughout the works.—Tbe Coroner: Is it net I' rola to provide changes of clothing for fitters—do you nevel do it P—Mr. Isherwood: I have never known it done. don't think it necessary that they should have a suit one- clothes, I have been in the place many times myself, Mr have brushed the chlorate off. There were other workmet.l employed there as well.—The Coroner: If a litter is es well as the grinder for a fortoight does not one man as much danger as the other P—Mr. Isherwood: Yea.-4ele" Coroner: Then why should one man only have a suit w clothes P—Mr. biberwood : I don't know; only that Oil, chlorate grinder is the regular man employed Coroner: If a man working there temporarily brusher/ 11,7 clothes does it take away the danger P—Mr.lsherwood: 497; I yes; I feel quite certain of that.—A Juror: I think quite necessary that all men working there should have " suit of clothes.—Mr. Isherwood: If they are only there le.; porarily a—The Juror: If they are only there an boor. 4 , should recommend that every person going there has a et o clothes—The Coroner, in summing up, remarked that:: could not see anyone was to blame for the death of '"'- deceased,, and he thought that the company would be anxious to prevent any future loss of life. He thought the., company would act on the suggestion of the jury if it thought necessary to provide a suit of clothes for ail= who vr,ould have to work in the department in question. jury could add a recommendation to that effect afitbeap, blame to anyone. He could not help thinking that large works it was all very well to say that a manager told, a man there was this danger and that danger, but line: bands were changed in the busy part of day, and lA% everything ,was bustle and excitement, it would be Inc f easier to say to a man "put on these clothes," inste giving them a lot of verbal instructions which they yoesi most likely forget the next minute.—The jury then retai° a verdict of "Accidental death," adding a recommendat''' that in tuttire a suit of clothes should be provided for or person who might boycott) work in the chlorate departoeonn —The Coroner (to Mr. Isherwood) : This does not that there it any blame attached to anyone.-Mr.laberro,,_ We shall be most happy to give effect to the recommepu tbe tion. We have only been anxious to do all we can funr_ ,_„. safety of the men.—The Coroner: We cannot help tb, 07 sometimes there is a great deal of negligence on b riti"e ',Ar. the men in carrying out the instructums given them. Isherwood : If we had anticipated anything of &hi-skin' should only have been toe glad to do it,

div.head: HATDOCK COLLIERS AND THEIR SICK FUND.
div.p: HATDOCK COLLIERS AND THEIR SICK FUND.
IMPORTANT DECISION.

An important case affecting the colliers of Haydock, Ashton, and G-olborne was heard at the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday afternoon, before T. P. E. Thomp- Esq., judge.—Messrs: Richard Evans and Company, of the Haydock Collieries, were sued by a collier named Dominick Traffelli (an Austrian) who claimed the sum of IN eld, alleged to be due uncier the rules of the Workmen's Sick and Burial Club, in connection with the collieries.—Mr. R. W. H. Thomas, solicitor, at. Helens, represented the plaintiff, and Mr. .1. 0. Swift, St. Helens, appeared for the defend- ants.—Mr. Thomas stated. that it was one of the rules con- nected with Messrs. Evan's collieries that all their work- men must be members of their sick club. The plaintiff went to work there on the 20th September last, and he was given a copy of the rules belonging to the sick club. One of the rules, No. 5, stated that Messrs. Richard Evans and Com- pany were to be treasurers, receive and pay all monies, and account for the same through the secretary. Rule 11th stated that " every full member, in case of sickness, shall be entitled to receive an allowance subject to rules hereinafter mentioned, at and after the rate of 10s. per week." The same rule also added that "-any new member shall not re- ceive any sick or funeral allowance until he or she has paid six weeks' contributions." The plaintiff went to work there on the 20th September lact, and worked for five weeks, re- I ceiving his wages weekly, and 3d per week deducted by the I colliery authorities as his contribution towards the sick club. They thus deducted five weeks' contributions, and the plaintiff went to work on the sixth week, but only worked one day, when he was taken ill. He sent in the, usual doctor's certificate to nay he was ill and unable to at- tend to his work; and on the settling day he sent for one day's wages, less his contribution to the sick club.- On the payment of that sixth weeks' contribution he would in the seventh week become entitled to receive sick benefit from the sick fund. But the authorities declined to deduct the sixth weeks' contribution from the one day's wage, and the result was that the plaintiff had not had any sick benefit.— I Dominick Traffelli, the plaintiff, was then called, and gave evidence in support of Mr. Thomas's statement. He eddedt that the defendants would neither pay back the Is 3d he had paid in contributions no;'- would they accept the sixth' weeks' 3d in order to make him entitled to the sick benefit. When he asked for the sick pay they told him he' was not entitled to any benefit—His Honour asked if they I stopped the 3d weekly from the wages of the men ?—Mr. rhomas replied in the affirmative.—Elis Honour: Then why I did they not stop the 3L.1 when there was only 4s due to him for this sixth week?—Mr. Swift: lain told they never de- stop anything for the club unless a man has to receive more than three days' wages.—His Honour: Can you show me a rule to that effect ?-41r. Swift: No.—Mr. Thomas: There is no rule to that effect. (To the plaintiff): Do you knew anything about having to work three days ?—The plaintiff: Oh, no, they never mentioned it to me.--His Honour (to Mr. Swift): If there had been such a rule here you would have been entitled to urge it, but I don't see how you can set up an additional rule that is not in the rules —Mr. Swift admitted that there was no such rule, but it was understood. —His Honour (to the plaintiff) Did you get your full 45.1 for the one day in the sixth week 2—The plaintiff: No, I only got 3s lid—thers was a penny stopped for oil.—ldis Honour Why did they not step the other 31 too.—Mr. Swift: Simply because of that rule, which is in operation in the colliery.—After a little further conversation, Mr. Swift said it was perfectly clear that the defendants were not liable to be sued. It was an unregistered society, and had no legal existence at all.—His Honour: Who is the person or body to be sued then P—Mr. Swift:l don't know that—His Hon- our: Surely Mr. Evans will not take that advantage P—Mr. Swift: He objects to being sued in a matter of dispute be- tween the members of this society. I was going to say that the affairs of this society are managed by 20 of the working men, and they have decided that this man has not to be paid, and Mr. Evans cannot take upon himself to pay it. Mr. Evans very naturally objects to having any judgment against him for this money. It is clear that unless a benefit or sick society is registered. neither the secretary, treasurer, nor anyone else can be sued.—His Honour: Messrs. Evass' act as treasurers, and receive and pay all money—Mr. Swift said no member of a society could sue the treasnrer or any- one, whatever his appointment was, unless the society had a legal constitution, and was registered under the Act of Parliament. He further maintained that the plaintiff had never paid his sixth week's contribution.—The plaintiff And they would never give me the chance.—His Honour rernuited that whoever was responsible he scarcely, thought they would take advantage of a man's informality or ignor-, ance.—Mr. Swift said the real question was, what was the intention of the rule; and he submitted that before any claim could be made upon the society a person must have worked and paid contributions for six full weeks. The object of the rule was to prevent any member claiming benefit immediately after joining: and it was a rule which the members themselves had made, and they were entitled to say they ought to be carried out.— His Honour : You admit that the practice was to deduct from the wages the contributions due 7—Mr. Swift: When a man has worked three days in one week; not where be was only one or two days at work. —Hie Honour: On what ground was it not deducted on this occasion ?—Mr. Swift: Because it is not the practice in this sick society or the Permanent Society to deduct any sick pay when a man has less than three days a week. Mr. Swift afterwards submitted that the plaintiff had not com- plied with the rules because he had not sent in a written notice of his sickness within twenty-four hoar.; whereupon Mr. Thomas said there were certain technical points in the case which he would admit, but he did not think the defendants were going to set them up.—His Honour said that the plaintiff was not really entitled to re- cover then.—Mr. Thomas said it was purely a technical ob- jection, and he did not think it ought to be insisted upon, especially as the plaintiff was a foreigner.—His Honour re- marked that according to the rules it seemed to him that the man's 3d. ought to have been received, and he would have then been entitled to his sick pay. He asked what would be done if a man received a knock on the head and wal insensible for a month.—Mr. Swift: There is a special provision with regard to accidents.—Mr. Thomas submitted that the doctor's certificate was sufficient notice of his ill- ness; but Mr. Swift quoted from the rules to show that the notice in writing must be apart from the medical cer- tificate.—Mr. Thomas thought it was only a frivolous ob- jection.—His Honour: It is a legal one. It depends on the goodwill of the people who have the administration of the fund whether the workmen shall have any benefit out of it or not.—Mr. Thomas: That is what it amounts to.— Hie Honour; In principle the man is entitled te his sick. pay, and his sixth week's contribution was due and ought to have been deducted.—Mr. Swift begged his Honour's pardon, and remarked that it was not due until the man had worked three days.—His Honour: It is due when the wages were paid for part of the sixth week, and the 3d. ought to have been taken out of the 4s.—Mr. Swift asked 116 Honour it he thought Wider the rules that a member was

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.

The Select Committee again met on Friday morning, when the examination of Mr. George Findlay, the general mana- ger of the London and North-Western Railway, was con- tinued. He said it was preposterous to suppose that if the canal were made salt would be sent to Manchester for transhipment whilst there was an almost free navigation direct to Liverpool. There was as much likelihood of a wood market being established at Bradford as at Man- chester. Manchester could never compete with Liverpool for the export trade of Yorkshire, Staffordshire, and Derby- shire, though he admitted that canals and the sea had e great tendency to reduce railway rates. For the export trade the railway rates were lower than those charged for goods for consumption in the centres of industry. he town and dock dues at Liverpool were very high, and with the exception of London it was the dearest port in the kingdom. He did not mean to say that the Dock Board had not laid out their estate in a way which they thought the most con- venient, but the connections between the docks and thi rail- ways were not as satisfactory as they might be. On Monday evidence was given hostile to the bill in be- half of landowners and residents on the proposed route. For Sir H. de Trafford it was stated that though Trafford Hall was not, perhaps, tke most desirable place of residence at present, yet the owner did not like the idea of quitting his family house. He did not wish to dispose of any of his land at Old Trafford, but desired to have added to his es- tate the portions of land which would be created if the canal were made. The works would add considerably to the in- convenience of approach to the hall. Mr. Foster, a civil engineer, said the Irwell below Manchester was "nothing but a common sewer," and if the Canal were constructed he anticipated great annoyance from the exhalations which would be given off by the foul and almost stagnant water. Professor Tidy, of the London Hospital, deposed to haying examined the Irwell water, which on his last inspection was in "about as horrible a state as could well be imagined," containing an enormous quantity of polluting matter. In his opinion it was " disgraceful " to allow the river to re- main in its present condition. Mr. Littler, Q.C., addressed the Committee in opposition to the bill. On Tuesday, Mr. Aspinall addressed himself to the evi- dence offered against the bill by the Corporations of Birken- head and Bootle, and by Miss Watt, a lady whose estate has a frontage to the Mersey of about three miles. He ques- tioned whether any company could be formed to carry out the project. The sole object of its existence, he maintained, was that Manchester might be saved some transit charges, whereas the petitioners desired to save Liverpool, Birken- head, and their incalculably valuable interests from almost certain injury.—Mr. Pember then commenced what he des- cribed as the appalling task of replying on the whole case in behalf of the promoters He emphasised their conten- tion that Lancashire and the counties immediately adjoining constituted the largest manufacturing centre in the world, and until lately enjoyed a supremacy now seriously threat- ened by dangers which, as had been consistently and con- scientiously urged, the canal would in part if not wholly remove. The opposition had been mainly that of persons reaping profits from taxes on industry, and the canal would confer an enormous boon upon consumers and producers alike if its only result was to break up the " ring " of Liverpool brokers. Mr. Pember's address, which included a remark that never in hiss xperience had a Parliamentary Committee better kept secret their ultimate intention, was not concluded when the Committee adjourned.

On Wednesday, Mr. Pember continued big closing speech in support of the bill. He maintained that the petitioners had not shaken the evidence of the promoters on any of the most material points, and he proceeded to show that there would be by means of this canal not only a saving of £508,000 a year on cotton, but an enormous saving on other commodities. With regard to the question of return cargoes from Manchester, the opponents had not produced a stronger case than that Of the promoters, and at all events it was shown that at present Liverpool sent away nearly 21 per cent. of her shipping in ballast. Mr. Hicks, an underwriter of Manchester, conclusively showed that the volume of trade for Manchester and the district would be 8,000,000 tons. It was anticipated also that Manchester would in- tercept the Wigan and South Yorkshire coal that was now sent to Liverpool for export. The contiguity of Manchester to the Cheshire salt districts was another important feature in the case. A million tons of salt were annually brought down the Weaver close to Manchester. He estimated that when the canal was made there would be an annual saving of £25,000 in the carriage of cattle and she.ip from Ireland for the Manchester and Salford markets. In fish, too, there would be a saving of 10s a ten on salmon alone from Scotland to Manchester. It was wrong to say that the whole of the capital would be raised in six months. But 80 completely did the promoters believe there was no danger about mining the capital that they would consent , to a clause providing that not a sod should be turned till five millions had been subscribed—not raised—because it I would be absurd' to raise it before it was wanted.—Mr. Pone De you mean subscribed by a contractor 7—Mr. Pember: No, I mean a clause providing without reservation that we I shan't turn a sod till five millions of capital have been sub- scribed. After arguing that the canal between the Mersey and Manchester contemplated by Parliament in the Acts passed 30 or 40 years was a ship canal and not a barge canal, the learned counsel ridiculed as preposterous the idea that the canal would not be able to compete with the railways. On Thursday morning Mr. Pember continued his reply, the Duke of Richmond again presiding. The learned gentleman said the last two points with which be had to deal were the estimates and the estuary works. In refe- rence to the first question he said that this being the se- cond year the promoters had been before Parliament they had paid special attention to the estimates, which, he said, were approved by engineers who had carried out similar works elsewhere. In one or two cases these eminent en- gineers were of opinion that the prices put down by Mr. Leader Williams were too high. He denied that the depre- ciation of dredging plant would, be as great as bad been suggested by Mr. Lyster and other engineers called by the Dock Board. One could not help feeling that Mr. Lyster went into this matter with a bias on the other side, and moreover, he set to work on the estimates for the express purpose of pulling them to pieces. The promoters' estimates were prima fade more trustworthy than the opponente' estimates for this reason—Mr. Leader Williams and the other engineers had their reputations at stake, and in fram- ing their estimates they knew well that their evidence would be sifted by hostile criticism in every particular. On the ether hand, the engineers for the opponents did all they could tP show that they were wrong. In the Canal proper and the dock works, however, their estimates were admitted en bloc, sad to that extent Mr. Williams' figures were un- challenged. He (Mr. Pember) argued from that fact that his other figures were right. He submitted that all the I evidence called by the opponents had broken down, becausel it was inconsistent itself. He now canto, and with full con- fidence, to.the estuary case, which would involve a greater amount of labour than any other part of the inquiry had done. If a mere expression of alas was to be enough to cause the rejection of the scheme, then he admitted that his efforts had been in vain. There was no use in arguing with a startled House. If Liverpool was afraid, and her fear was to be enough to upset all they hoped to do on the Mersey, then he might as well give up further effort. In conclusion, he said Manchester wanted the river to be better than it now was, and would shrink from no act of co-operation to im- prove the river or enlarge its capacity. Great interests bad been proved and great destinies had been shown to be im- perilled. The commercial interests of England were at stake. The contest was one of resolution against timorous netts, energy against apathy, progress against retrogression Their Lordships would not be slow to see that, and be left with all confidence the determination in their hands.—Tbe Committee retired at half•past four and returned after an absence of a few minutes, when the Chairman announced that as the case was one of great importance the Committee would like time to consider. They would meet next morn- ing at eleven, and after considering the matter would at once deliver their decision.—The Committee then ad- journed.

WIT AND HUMOUR.

A Gaamnruf. CounscrioN.-.--" The proper study of man- kind is woman." What part of a dwelling-house would best snit a phreno- logist for his study 7—The scullery. Man's happiness is said to hang upon a thread. This mast be the thread that is never at hand to sew on the shirt. button that is always off. "John," said the hotel-steward to the store-room man, "hand me that bottle of cider. I am going to give them some Madeira sauce to-day." " Yon're the most curious woman I ever heard of," said a boy to his mother—" you tell me I have a bad temper, and yet blame me for losing it! " A German physician defines the main difference between the effects of whiskey and beer to be—" Visky makes you kill somebody else; mit beer you only kills yourself." Schoolmistress: "You see, child, if I puncture this india- rubber ball, it will collapse. Do you understood 7" Child: " Oh, yes, I understood! If you prick it, it will go squash." "And do your workmen," asked a London visitor of a Lancashire mill-owner, "really live in those hovels? " "Certainly not," replied the master. "They only sleep there. They live in my mill." Co.—What difference is there in the way in which men and women show their love for each other? Why, when a man is in love with a woman, he throws himself at her feet; but, when a woman is in love with a man, she throws herself at his head. "Yes," said the society young man, "I think she is in- deed a charming girl, and such a brilliant conversationalist I talked with her for upwards of ten minutes the other evening, and we referred to the weather only once during the whole time." JONATHAN IN SWITZERLAND.—There is something ex- quisitely cool in the following reply of a Yankee to a European traveller when he asked him if he had just crossed the Alps—" Wall, now you call my atten- tion to the fact, I guess I did pass risin' ground 1" "My son," said an old negro," now dat you's outen de penitentiary, try ter keep out, an' arter dis doan steal—least- wise dean du lack yer did befo', steal a pair o' boots wat was too big fur yeself an' too little fur yer old daddy. Ef yer kaint pick up authin' dat'll do yer some good, try an' be hones'. Two Parisian students who were not rolling in wealth used to go each morning in turn to buy provisions for the day. One day he whose turn it was to make the purchases had hardly put two cutlets upon the table before the cat grabbed one and ran away with it. 'A h," said he to his friend, "the cat has run away with your cutlet!" Doctor Chalmers, when once invited to address a primi- tive prayer meeting in a remote Highland parish, was re- quested to "speak down" to the intelligence of his flock, and use only the simplest words and sentences. Chalmers good- naturedly assented, and began with this easy sentence —"My friends, I have been specially requested, in addressing you to-night, to avoid the technical nomenclature of scholastic theology." At a certain Australian hotel colonial beer is sold at three- pence the imperial pint; and the local paper tells how two gentleman were talking together over their glass,when one of them hazarded the opinion that at such a price the ale could not possibly be good. The remark was overheard by an old man who, in a very advanced state of inebriety, was stand- ing at the bar enjoying his cheap beer. "Not good, gen'le• nen ?" said he. "You're mistaken. Look at me for nine- Pence !" Par's WETTING.—The proprietor of a shooting-box in the West of Ireland, having been driven home in a regular down- Pour, and perceiving that his Jahn was almost in rags, sympathetically said, "Pat, my poor fellow, you must be Wet through and through!" "Faith, then, ne, your honour," leplied Pat; "I am wet only to the skin; but plase goodness, be wet inside as soon as your honour can get out the aperrits !"

The innovation Was a startling one, and the sixth form offered to it a passive rnsistance which, considering the nature of the text-book lhaployed, Russell's Modern Europe, was, from a literary ' :utetorical point of view, not altogether indefensible, ffilt finding his questions very readily answered, the doctor en One occasion asked, as a sort of final question, and in a voice of, for him, somewhat unusual sternness," And how; Marls, did the Huns conduct themselves after their arrival in Italy ?" The answer, given verbatim from the text-book, and sounding all the more absurd from the relentless accu- racy with which the author's almost incredible sentence had been committed to nninory, and the calm deliberation with which the words were uttered, ran as follows—" They hunted the bear in the voluptuous parterre, the trim gardea, And the expensive pleasure-ground , where effeminacy was Wait to saunter and indolence to loll." The Liverpool Review of Saturday last contains the /allowing remarks on the Runcorn Commissioners —"At: the last monthly meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners the statement was made that the cost of the agents and solicitor in conducting the business of the Board in relation to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill amounted to £l4O 6d. 2d (not 6s 8d); the cost of the deputation to Lon- don and Manchester ainoanted to a further SIM Of £7B 14s 2d, total £214 Os 4d, Some economical people have ueen heard to say that the odd four-pence mentioned in the total was quite enough to pay for the benefit the town will ever receive from the concessions said to have been obtained from the promoters of the bill. Such a cruel remark must have been very unpleasant to the three gentlemen deputed to the Lords' Committee on such a delicate mission. Ac- cording to their own account their display of diplomatic skill must have been something astounding. It is singular what a taste this Board has developed of late for legal pro- ceedings, which, it is needless to say, are of a costly charac- ter. The celebrated 'Beasley case,' which cost the town over £l,OOO, still rankles in the righteous bosoms of many in- dignant ratepayers. And there is every reason to believe that they have only continued to touch the fringe of the canal question. It must not he supposed that these clever Commissioners are a spendthrift set. Their pet pleasure is law, and in order to enjoy themselves in that direction they economise in every otner department they have to control. It is the ambition of every Commissioner to be on the Legal and Parliamentary Committee. Many people are sur- prised at the passion for law and other eccentricities, not in an economical direction, that are developed by the locJ governing body at Runcorn. There is no occasion for sur- prise. The result is quite a natural one. The Commis- sioners are members for life. The chemical works of the dis- trict form an interest so great that no one who is obnoxious to the powers that ' can ever hope to be elected, and therefore men without back-bone are at the behest of the reigning Chemical Monarch put on the Boardl and if they never commit the blunder of having an idea of their own they are left in undisturbed possession of their seats and the doubtful honour the position carries with it. Some people are weak enough to suppose that if the system of election by means of the ballot were adopted there would be an alteration for the better. Nothing of the sort. The town is utterly demoralised so far as its public spiiit is concerned. Runcorn seems to be in a bad way, and if the good old ship is not to be left stranded, she will have to put on all sail. With a good helmsman, and an abl•hodied crew, she may get abreast of the times in days to come. But where is the helmsman? And where could be found the crew."

div.head: ASSAULT.
div.p: ASSAULT.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions," -on Monday, before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell and Mr. A. Thomas, Mr. Peter Smith, of the firm of Messrs. Smith and Co., chemists and druggists, Bridge-street, was summoned to answer a charge of assault- ing and beating Albert Ellis—The defendant pleaded not guilty.—The complainant, who is le years of age, said he was in Mr. Smith's employ, and drove his horse and cart. On Tuesday, the 13th inst., Mr. Smith sent him to the rail- way station for some goods, and on returning along Low- lands•road the bearing rein slipped off the saddle. He got upon the horse's back to put it right, when a dog he had in the cart followed him, and the horse ran about 20 yards, although he was pulling back at the reins. Mr. Ball saw him, and said he wou'd have the mare lamed, fie took the goods to the shop, and Mr. Smith sent him to the top locks. When he returned to the stable, Mr. Smith took hold of his ear and asked what he had been doing. As he was telling him, Mr. Smith struck him with his fist and punched him two or three times. Mr. Smith strack him in the eye.—The defendant said he had a witness who would contradict the statements of the complainant, and their wor- ships would see that it was a very paltry affair. He had simply chastised the lad moderately for doing wrong. The horse the boy was driving was a valuable animal, between four and five old, and in the cart he had a fox terrier, which he had ao right to have. In the neighbourhood of the station the boy got upon the horse's back and enticed the dog after him. As soon as the horse felt the boy and dog on its back and the cart behind it the animal naturally commenced kicking, and ran away for a considerable dis- tance, the boy having no control whatever over the animal. Under these circumstances many casualties might have oc- curred. Somebody might have been killed, and he (Mr. Smith) might have been placed in the same position as Mr. Jackson, whose horse whilst in charge of a servant ran away and killed a child. As it was the cart was damaged. His (Mr Smith's)only remedy was either to dismiss the boy or to chastise him moderately, and he administered such punish- ment as a father would to a son, or a master to an appren- tice, simply for the lads own good. If the lad's eye had been discoloured, it was certainly not by being atruck, but by falling off the horse.—Ellis was then charged with being in such a position that he could not have proper direction over the horse.—Mr. J. Ball, shipbroker, said he was walk- ing from the railway station on Tuesday morning when he saw Mr. Smith's cart standing near the gate. The lad was on the horee'a back and persuading the dog to jump on also. At last the dog did jump on the horse's back, and immedi- ately the animal started off and ran for a distance of 150 yards, when the lad got upon the home's shoulder and man- aged to stop her.—By Mr. Smith : The lad had not hold of the reins.—Mr. Smith said the horse was a very quiet but a valuable one, and such a thing would not have occur- red if the lad had used ordinary precautions.—The Chair- man said the Bench considered the boy's conduct such that the assault went for nothing, and the charge against Mr. I Smith was dismissed. The boy had conducted himself with a valuable horse in a very reprehensible way, and most people would have treated him worse than Mr. Smith had done. He might have caused a serious accident through his carelessness and neglect, and they should fine him Is and costs 15s, to let boys and apprentices know that they could not play tricks with valuable horses, and other property placed in their charge. He deserved more than ha got in the way of a thrashing, and lie was now further punished and his mother also, for the Bench considered her to blame for bringing the case before the court.
