Sir,—lt is somewhat surprising that your correspondent, "A Parishioner," could not give expression te his sentiments as to the difference between parson and schocffinaster at Stocktoa Reath, without endeavouring to offend non- Churchmen, and that stir up increased sectarian bitterness between one body and another of the Stockton" Heathens." As the only public elementary school in the place is that in conneciion with the Cuurch, the children of Dissenters attend perforce in considerable numbers, and as parents are generally allowed, "A Parishioner" notwithstanding, to take some little interest in the education of their children, I cannot see, that it is any way singular that non-Churchmen should sign a petition in favour of a schoolmaster in whose hands they are content to leave the education of their chit- dren, and in disparagement of whose abilities even " Parishioner," with all his bitterness and cynicism," has not one word to say." Perhaps "A Parishioner," in his next essay, will kindly give us his reasons why non-Churcbtnen should not sign- such a petition. Is it because the school in nominally a Church school ? I say nominally, for it is well known in the parish that with the exception of a confirmation class the Vicar has not given a Scripture lesson in either day or %Sunday school since his appointment. This may be owing to the severity of his other duties, i r,. preaching, pastoral visitation, Jo., rkc. ; but it is pretty certain that had the religious teaching of the schools been, more dog- matic than it is at present the children of Dissentsrs would have been conspicuous (like "A Parishioner" en Sundays). by their absence. Non-Churchmen have more congdence in , the fairness and fitness of trained lay teachers to impart 'scriptural instruction to their children than in the modem- tiOn of parsons. " A Parishioner's" malicious hints that the school mana- gers out of kindness to Mr. Tirnson have kept back the re- cital of some serisna offences, do not impose upon the parishioners who have better opportunities for kuo ming his whole course of conduct than the "many leading towns- men" who dwell in an upper and more sereoe ;atmosphere, and derive their information at second-band. Disputes, ex- cite comparisons which in this case are not in favour of "the black dragoon." ' 1 have heard a story of a curate vtl;% asked his bishop or prefermect, and being requested to give some proof of tae soundness of his claim, replied that he had been ordained an many years and thus thought his, turn was due, "That is not what i mean "• replied the bishop, "I want to know what increase of nutnbers has there been in your church, what aggressive work c irried on?" "Oh, my lord,' responded the curate, "I cannot say much about those things, but I have succeeded in estiblistainr, an ex- Oellent trass band !" That curate Went empty away. I leavd "a Parishioner" to thaw his own moral.
RUSTIO.

Sir,—Perinit me to bear testimony to Cute correctness of the paragraph in your issue of the loth ins,.ant, which should not lead to any misapprehension whatever. Why 0, Parishioner " should sty that your informant, whoever he „Hy be, baa wilfu!ly misrepresented the case, or that he was in ignorance of facts, I fait to ere In saying there are no strained relations I think " Parishioner " is altogether mis- taken. Does he requie soca indecent scenes as have dis- grace! the agitation at Earlestmen to prove the sincerity of the sympathy for Mr. "Nilson ? Th se who feel strongest In the matter are most des;rous not to incur the odium Which always attaches to those who create a disturbance ' even when they are in the right. I would line to ask if the meetiug at which Mr. Timson was disinissed was not c riled in a very hasty and extraordi- 'rare manner. The grievance h tppened at about nine o'clock on Friday night, and his dismissal was decided upon the following Saterd ay afternoon. Did not the majwity of the managers attend toe meeting with their minds alrea ly pre- parA for the business ? The vicar might have retired from the chair while his grievance was being diecussed, for every- one knows what n clerical chairman means in parochial matters. and this is even more fully 'expel irruced in country villages such as the one in cpmetmn. Mr. Nilson was not allowed tat be present to hear the charge laid against him, though called in afterwards and asked what lie had to say—the semb'ance of jastice without the re ,lity. tie was then requested to retire, awl the vicar remained as accuser and judge. Yet the public are asked to believe that the vicar was not con- cerned. The churchwardens tone of whom heard what transpired on the Friday evening in question) deClined follow up the action of the uwirigers and dismiss Mr. rim- son from hi a position as organist. so the whole affair lay in abeyance until after the Easter vestry. when that particular warden (the vicar's) was put out of office, and another, a school manager, instituted. The other churchwarden in also a manager. A few elays after the vestry bith positions- ' were advertised, four m'Onths or more having elapsed since Mr. liaison received notice sor the school. When the post of organist was advertised, Mr. Thnson bad not received notice for the same. I think this action sp.aks for itself. I ask, hoc's not the managers acted entirely on the vicar'n representation? ' It seems to me to be evident from "Parishioner's" remarks that he himself iA ain anager. If Any statements are veiled or imputations made-it is by " Parishioner." ff:e prebably refers to a lifference between the vicar and Mr. Timson over two years ago. The facts of the case are briefly theqe. Mr. Tionson feeling aggrieved at certain threats the vicar had used to him, consul•ed one of the mahaors, who said he wou'd ingaire into it at their next meeting. At this meeting the vie ir gave his version of the affair while Mr. Timson was not in the room, and must have reoresented to ahem that Mr. ?mason was the offender, though be said be should not have mentioned it, if Mr. Tirnson had net caused it to he brought forward, and ultim,tely the matter fell through, it being understood that it 8 mould not be spoken of to outsiders. Certainly at this meeting one mauager proposed that Mr. Timeon should write an apology or be ngarsted to resign. brit it ended there. It is by re-openinu this that " Parishioner " leads me to think he must he manager. I proftat• toe, against Parishioner veiling this trivial in it- ter in uch strong language, so as to set the public Mind s wandering after some serious offence on the part of Mr. cimsnn. He knows a statement of the facto would prove the weakness of the case. Yours Italy, May 22nd, 1884. FAIR PLAY.

THE STOCKTON HEATIT DISPUTE.

The position of affairs as regards this dispute is as yet unchanged. As far as can be 8€3,-11 there are no signs of an amicable arrangement being arrived at. On the one hand those who have at present control of the schools seem die- posed to exert their "little brief authority to the utmost, I while on the other hand the supporters of Mr. Timson, who consider themselves strong in a just cause, seem determined to use all legitimate means to prevent what they hold to be an ,injustice being done. No answer to, nor even an acknowledg- ment of the receipt of, the numerously signed petition which was sent to them has been received from the vicar and his col- leagues on the board of management of the school, and this want of ordinary courtesy, it is needless to say, has not tended to alley the exaeperation of the popular party. In the meantime the public interest in the matter is shown in many ways, and perhaps as much as any by the amount of comment evoked by two sermons preached by the vicar on Sunday. These, it may at once be admitted, would under ordinary circumstances have passed as ordinary sermons; but in the present somewhat exceptioual state of affairs they have been construed as being specially intended to fortify his supporters. The morning's discourse in particular, which was suggested by the text. "That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men and cunning craft nesl, whereby they lie in wait to deceive." It contained- . Many examples of the evil constquences of want of firmness of purpose. It has been taken as designed "ta encourage the others," "the others" twit g some of the colleagues of the reverend gentleman who have been somewhat influenced by the vox populi. Of course, it is possible that these epteulations owe as much to the imagination of those who entertained them as to any real knowledge of the object of the seemons in question, but at the same time they shove what a strong interest is taken in the dispute.

The clauses are now being prepared. It is stated that the £5,000,000 is assured already, and that the canal committee deem the condition in no way onerous. . .

SIR GILBERT GREENALL AND TORY .INTIMI- DATION. Sir,--The old saying "Scratch's', Tory and you will find a tyrant" has just received ample illustration in the speech of the Tory candidate at the recent hybrid workingmen s(?) !meting. Sir Gilbert is never tired of telling us that he lathe workingman's friend, and so he is, as long as the working- man will help to swell his profits by drinking Wilderspool ale, and is ready to allow his own personality to become completely absorbed in the glorious light of the Tory can- didate's Intellectuali:y. But let a poor fellow, under the impression that he lives in a land of freedom and is pos- sessed of the rights of citizenship, venture to criticise the conduct of this great paragon of Tory excellenc., and what I happens? From that moment he becomes the object of Sir Githert's bitter (Belize. A few weeks ago one "Thomas Flood" wrote a letter, in which he mercilessly exposed the fallacy of Sir Gilbert's supposed generosity, and at every Tory meeting since poor " Flood" has come in for a torrent of abuse which is more remarkable for showing evidences of bad grammar, bad taste, and insane attempts ; at wit, than anything else. Now, if the matter b....ft re- mained here no harm would have been done, but "Flood " happens to be an employe of a company with which Sir Gil., bert's firm do business. By the Way, the statement that Sir ' Gilbert's various concerns are the largest supporters of the London and North-Western Railway Company in Warring- ton, is a pure invention, and I happen to know has no foundation in fact. Therein one firna alone whose carriage account is at least four or five times as large, and numbers of ethers who pay considerably more than the brewery doer, However, Sir Gilbert evidently thinks that be can compel the directors of the largest commercial concern in the kingdom, out of deference to his business connection to do his behests by coercing poor " Flood " into silence. Are the workingmen of Warrington, Liberals and Tories alike, so blind as to permit one of their own order to be trampled on in this fashion? I think not; and the next general election will show that the speech of last Monday has put a good many nails into the political coffin of the Tory party in Warrington. Now, as to the Fishing. Itirt a curious fact that it should be only now discovered that the fish are too small, and consequently must not be caught. Why, we all know per- fectly well that the Reservoir is simply " snowing " with ' fish at the present moment, and it is nothing but the selfish- ness of the owner which closed the place to the public some time ago, and has kept it closed ever since. Out upon such conduct! Does Gilbert (Treenail think the fishermen of Warrington are a lot of children ? But what about thp new Corrupt Practices Act? Will it not cover the " Fish ' and the "Fload" at the same time ? Has Sfr Gilbert ever heard about the "Rabbits" at Launceston? Where was his "keeper "—I Leg pardon—his "legal adviser " last Mon- day, that he did not prevent his patron from committing himself so foolishly ? It seems to me that every fresh ex- hibition of the "odd old man" is making the task of the Liberal party easier than before—Yours,ANTl-HUMBHG. P.S.—The speakers had a good deal to say at the meet- ing about the Liberal majority baying been .reduced from 130 to 28, but what now when it has gone up to 195?

TIIE REPRESENTATION OE WARRINGTON. We are glad to be able to state that the committee ap- pointed by the Warrington Liberal Association to consider the question of a suitable candidate to contest Witl rington in the Liberal interest, have succeeded in obtaining the con- sent or Mr. William Crosfield, of Liverpool, whose name will accordingly, within the next few days, be submitted to I a general meeting of the Association for approval. Mr. I Crosfield, it may be mentioned, is a cousin of the Messrs Crosfield, so well-known in this town as large employers of labour and thorough-going supporters of the Liberal cause. 'Mr. Croefield occupies a piominent position in Liverpool as a successful merchant, and also as a promoter of philanthropic and religious objects. It is therefore likely that he will, when the matter is submitted to the , general meeting, receive the cordial support of the whole of the party. We may explain to avoid a misconception which prevails in soine quarters that other tree gentlemen only besides Mr. W. Crostield have been invited to allow their names to be brought before the members of the Liberal Association. One of these was Mr. John Croefield, wheee consent, it is needless to say, the Liberals of Warrington would have been extremely pleased to obtain, but it was ; found that belied insuperable objections to 'being put fir- ward as a candidate for Parliamentary honours. Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., as reported last week, was the next I gentleman consulted, and he expressed himself fully sensi- ble of the honour done to him by the invitation to become A candidate for such an important borough, but having re- gard te the work at present being carried on in Ipswich, his present seat, and the confidence and sympathy he had !'secured in that borough, he felt obliged to agein place his services at the disposal of his present constituente. Mr. William Crosfield has, as we have stated, responded at "the third time of asking," and we trust the result will be a happy Parliamentary union with Warrington. At the last moment, we learn that a special meeting of the General Council will be held on Wednesday evening next in Wycliffe Hall. The business, as stated by the cir- cular is :.—"To receive the report and recommendation of the sub-cominittee appointed by the General Council, and to decide what course of action shall be adopted is reference thereto." The meeting is called by the President, Mr. S. Rigby, J.P., and Mr. McMinnies, M.P., will also be present.

ANOTHER CHURCH AND SOEMOIJ DISPUTE NEAR WARRINGTON. Disputes in matters pertaining to the Established Church threaten to become, as it were, epidemical in this neighbour- hood. The latest outbreak has occurred at Strettou and is in many of its aspects similar to that which is at present disturbing the adjoining parish of Stockton Reath, though it is only fair to say it has not, and it may be hoped will not, reach such an acute stage as the latter. In %ach case the cause of the dispute is the dismissal of the schoolmaster of the National School, who is also (in each case) organist of the parish church. At Stretton, we understand, the manage- ment of the schools 'Maud has been hitherto practically in the hands of the vicar, for as to such board of managers as there may be, it may be said that "they come like shadows, so depart." Within the past few weeks a letter determining his engagement has been sent to the schoolmaster, Mr. J. Ellison' by the Rev. Canon Dodd, the vicar, without however, fixing any definite time at which Mr. Ellison is to yield up Cis office. On this actipn on the part of the vicar becoming known throughout the parish, it appears to have given considerable dissatisfaction, the services of Mr. Ellison apparently having, on the whole, won the approval of the parishioners. The feeling of his parishioners waare- presented to Canon Dodd, who it must in fairness be men- tioned has shown a more conciliatory spirit twin his neigh.. , boor. The notice of dismissal has, however, we believe, not 1 yet been withdrawn, but it is strongly hoped that a sem- i promise will be arrived at which will be satisfactory to hoar parties. It is understood that ths chief cause of complaint, which Canon Dodd puts forward aeainet Mr. Ellison is with regard to the manner in which he plays the organ and con- ducts the choir. On the other hand it is contended by Mr. Ellison's supporters that this part of his duties is performed to the satisfaction of the congregation and with as much efficiency as can be expected for the remuneration given to him as organist; and some even go IC. far as to say that the aloe of organist of the parish church is only of minor im- portance as compared with that of school teacher, and that any little deficiency in that respect ought not to act the position of a schoolmaster who, appears, to give satisfaction throughout the parisn.

SERMON 3 Sunday School anniversary sermons in connection with the Wesleyan Chapel of Partington were preached on Sunday lasr,, to large congregation., by the Rev. Allen Rees, of Bowdon. The discourses were practical and comprehensive, and were listened to with marked atten- tion. The collections were about ten pounds. TBA MISSTING, isc.—The Theological Class in connection with the We-lean Chapel had on Wednesday evening its social tea in the large vestry, when there WAS a good attend- ance. An excellent tea was provided by Miss Owen, to which ample jo.tice was done. A meeting was afterwards held, presided over by the president, the Rev. R. Dillon, when there were addresses sod singing. Testimony was given of the great good the young people had derived from the class. It was res dyed by united eff wt to render the class a still greeter success. A most enj.yable evening was spent, the mernhers arp.titing full of hope for the future. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. The Earl of Deut.norsin, replying to the Earl of Rose., bery, said the report of the sub conunittee appointed to in- quire as to the best position of Scotitsh Harbours of Refuge, was in the printer's hands —Earl Gitantrimm stated that the House would rise on Tuesday for the Whitsuntide re- cess which would terminate on the 16th June.—The second reading of the Settlement and Removal Law Amendment Bill was posrponed.—The House considered the report of tlite Criminal Law Amendment Bill. GENERAL GORDO/V.—Earl GRANVILLE, replying to Earl Galloway, said the latest direct information from General Gordon was dated the 10th inst. A telegram had that even- ing been received from Mr. Egerton, stating that the Mudeer of Dongola had got a messenger into Khartoum, but the messenger could not leave. He could give no ad- ditional information respecting the Government intentions or respecting General Gordon.—The Colonial Prisoners Re- moval Bill passed through Committee.—The House ad- journed.
